CONSENSUS SURVEYS
       You’re all set to go out for a leisurely walk. Weather forecasters have predicted sunny
       skies and warm temperatures, so you head out in shorts and leave the sweater at home.
       Ten minutes later a heavy thunderstorm erupts, followed by colder air. You quickly
       scramble back for a change of clothing, all the while cursing the forecasters. How could
       they have gotten it so wrong?
           Money managers encounter similar experiences, except that instead of weather
       reports, they tend to rely on surveys that feature forecasts from experts on what an
       upcoming economic indicator will report. If the actual economic news falls in line with
       expectations, there is generally little market reaction to the news because investors
                                       Moving Average                                         23



   already anticipated it. By getting it right, those forecasters demonstrated that they have a
   good grasp on what the economy is up to. However, had the news about the economy
   turned out to be radically different from what private experts predicted, money managers
   would have rushed in to readjust their investment positions. These abrupt moves can
   potentially shake up the value of stocks, bonds, and currencies. Why such violent market
   reactions? Any major departure from expectation means that something is going on in the
   economy for which the experts failed to account. Naturally, this creates fresh uncertainty
   about current and future economic conditions. The bigger the gap between consensus
   expectations and reality, the larger the backlash in the financial markets.
        Who puts out these consensus surveys, and how are they done? Many financial wire
   service organizations, such as Bloomberg, Dow Jones, Reuters, and Market News
   International, produce their own consensus surveys by polling economists for their pre-
   dictions on key upcoming economic indicators. These indicators include consumer prices,
   producer prices, industrial production, retail sales, capacity utilization, and others. The
   methodology used is fairly simple: The responses of individual business economists are
   basically averaged out, and that becomes the consensus forecast.

MOVING AVERAGE
   There’s great temptation to jump to a conclusion about the economy’s health from just
   one month’s data, but that’s not a wise practice. Economic numbers can be faulty, inaccu-
   rate, or, at the very least, misleading because of unusual events such as a major labor
   strike or severe weather conditions. Such situations can diminish the reliability of an eco-
   nomic indicator in the short term, so it’s important to use caution when extrapolating
   information from just a single month’s data.
        To get a truer sense of the underlying trend in the economy, it’s far better to rely on a
   moving average of economic numbers. Simply put, a moving average is a computation in
   constant motion because it always averages data for the most recent fixed number of
   months. As a result, the average changes with the introduction of each new monthly
   report. For example, let’s say consumer price inflation shot up 1% in the most recent
   month. Obviously, a rise of that magnitude could raise lots of red flags. However, before
   anyone panics, it’s far more prudent to consider inflation’s actual trend by looking at its
   moving average over the past three or six months. To do this, simply add up the inflation
   changes over the past three or six months and divide by the total number of months you
   considered. When the next set of inflation figures is released a month later, recalculate the
   moving average by including the new figure in the equation and discarding the oldest
   monthly data so that you are always averaging the latest three- or six-month periods.
   The virtue of moving averages is that they smooth out random fluctuations and make
   long-term trends clearer. One disadvantage of a moving average is that it’s a lagging indi-
   cator. Averages are slower to respond when there’s a genuine change in the economy’s
   direction.
24                    Chapter 2 • A Beginner’s Guide: Understanding the Lingo



NOMINAL DOLLARS VERSUS REAL DOLLARS (ALSO KNOWN AS CURRENT
DOLLARS VERSUS CONSTANT DOLLARS)
     Anything measured in dollars can be looked at in two ways. Nominal dollars (also
     referred to as current dollars) represents the actual amount of money spent or earned over
     a period of time. You’ll see stories mentioning how American factory workers received
     total pay hikes of $500 million, or a 5% increase, in the past 12 months. Or perhaps you
     read that company A reported that income from sales of sweaters climbed to $220 million
     that year, up from $200 million the year before, or a jump of 10%. These figures are
     based in nominal dollars.
          However, nominal (or current) dollars gives you only part of the story. What’s miss-
     ing is how inflation can distort such numbers. Let’s go back to the example of the earn-
     ings of factory workers. They might have seen their pay jump by 5% in nominal terms,
     but before anyone celebrates, someone should ask this question: “What if the price of
     goods and services (that is, inflation) rose by 4% during that same period?” In that case,
     the wages of these workers rose by a less-than-impressive 1% in real (or constant) dollars.
     In other words, the actual increase in purchasing power these workers gained from their
     pay hike was far smaller than 5%.
          Let’s now look at company A. It noted that sales revenue jumped by 10%. However,
     that doesn’t necessarily mean it sold 10% more sweaters. In fact, the firm ended up sell-
     ing the same number of sweaters both years. The only reason it received more money in
     the second year is because the company raised the price of sweaters by 10%. Thus, the
     increase in real (constant) dollar sales was actually zero!
          Nominal dollars simply reflects the present value of goods and services exchanged in
     the marketplace. However, real dollars tells you the true value of goods and services pro-
     duced or sold, because it strips out the effects of inflation. When economists and
     investors want to compare the economy’s performance over different time frames, they
     generally look at both measures—nominal and real. They note the change in the size of
     the economy in nominal dollars because that points to what individuals, businesses, and
     the government actually spent. However, to find out whether the economy genuinely
     expanded by producing more in quantity or volume, economists and investors look at the
     numbers in real-dollar terms.

REVISIONS AND BENCHMARKS
     Traders and money managers are always hungry for the very latest piece of economic
     news. The more timely the information, the more influential it is; and the faster investors
     can get their hands on it, the quicker they can act.
          Therein lies the problem. Government agencies and private groups that supply eco-
     nomic data to the public are under tremendous pressure to get it out quickly, and that’s
     not easy. Every week or month, depending on the economic indicator, statisticians follow
                                     Seasonal Adjustments                                      25



   a rigid schedule to query sources in the field, collect the raw responses, organize the data,
   readjust for seasonal factors, perhaps recalculate the numbers to adjust for inflation, and
   then write some introductory comments about the results before finally releasing the data
   to the public. It’s a hurried process in which accuracy and completeness at times take a
   back seat to getting the information out on deadline. For this reason, the first release of
   many economic indicators contains pieces of data that are far from reliable and thus are
   considered preliminary.
        Of course, to many investors, it makes little difference whether the initial data is reli-
   able. They trade on these numbers anyway, because the figures represent the very latest
   information they can get on the economy. Later, though, as more information is received
   and after statisticians have had a chance to review their computations, the preliminary fig-
   ures undergo one or more revisions. Though investors also see the revisions to earlier
   data, they generally do not spark much trading because by then the information refers to a
   time period that has long since passed. Investors usually focus on the future, not the past.
   Economists, however, take revisions more seriously because the new figures can affect
   their forecasts of economic activity.
        Benchmark changes are different from monthly revisions. The latter are an ongoing
   effort to make the statistical results more accurate, especially if there was insufficient
   time to gather all the data. In contrast, benchmark changes occur about once a year or so,
   when the government introduces new seasonal adjustment factors or decides to undertake
   a formal change in the methodology itself. Benchmark revisions can affect economic data
   going back five, ten, or even more years to allow for historical comparisons.

SEASONAL ADJUSTMENTS
   Before most economic indicators are released, they are calculated to reflect seasonal
   adjustments. What are seasonal adjustments? The simplest way to answer this question is
   with an example. It’s no surprise that consumers do a lot more shopping during the
   November/December holiday period than at other times of the year. In addition, when the
   Christmas shopping season is over, retail sales often slow in January and February. These
   seasonal shifts in consumer spending patterns are quite common. They’re temporary
   changes that have nothing to do with the business cycle.
         Let’s look at another example. In the spring when schools let out, the number of peo-
   ple getting jobs surges as students enter the workforce to earn money over the summer.
   By mid-August, the process is reversed, and employment drops off as students leave the
   workforce and return to school. Again, these fluctuations in employment are perfectly
   normal and do not indicate a fundamental change in the economy’s health. Even indus-
   trial production tends to fall in July as automakers shut down plants that month to retool
   their assembly lines for the new model year. No one should conclude that this slowdown
   in industrial output means that the manufacturing sector is in trouble. These are all rou-
   tine seasonal shifts that take place in the economy.
26                    Chapter 2 • A Beginner’s Guide: Understanding the Lingo



          How do you differentiate changes that are the result of normal seasonal factors from
     those that represent a more serious problem in the economy? That’s where the seasonal
     adjustment process comes in. Government experts look at economic data going back five
     to ten years to identify recurring trends. These trends are changes in economic activity
     that have nothing to do with the broader business cycle but that can be explained by short-
     term external factors (such as summers, winters, and major holidays). After observing
     such patterns, officials come up with a formula that factors out variations in the economic
     numbers attributable to seasonal changes. This enables private economists and investors
     to distinguish economic events that should be viewed as normal from those that are out of
     the ordinary.
          Seasonal adjustments, however, are far from perfect. You could have abnormal eco-
     nomic data even after seasonal adjustments are considered, and it still doesn’t necessarily
     signal a turning point in the economy. Blizzards, floods, terrorism, labor strikes, and
     major bankruptcies are all unpredictable shocks that can have an impact on economic out-
     put, but their effects are almost always short-lived. Moreover, these incidents are easy to
     identify as the cause of any sharp deviation in business activity. By and large, seasonal
     adjustments are important to analysts because they can help identify true deviations from
     the normal course of activity in the economy.
          Now that we have reviewed some of the most widely used terms that accompany eco-
     nomic indicators, we’re ready to move on to the next chapters. What are the world’s most
     influential economic indicators, and how do you get the most out of these statistics? How
     do you locate them? Interpret them? Most important of all, where can you find the clues
     that can tip you off to how the economy might perform in the future?
                        The Great Recession of 2008–2009                                  27




The Great Recession of 2008–2009
The cause and severity of the Great Recession (December 2007 to June 2009) can be
traced to acts of colossal human folly. These acts, which include fraud, recklessness,
greed, and the laxness of regulators, so damaged the U.S. economy that they left more
than 15 million people jobless, destroyed $16 trillion in household wealth, forced a
record 46 million Americans into poverty, and caused an unprecedented number of
families to lose their homes. You might well ask, “How could this have happened to a
modern, high-tech, presumably well-informed economy?” The answer is disturbingly
plain: Though the U.S. economy has many great attributes, hubris and stupidity
inevitably trump all.
Though economic historians will long debate the precise origins of this recession, here
is a rough sequence of events that doomed the economy to its most destructive fall in
more than half a century:
    1. For years Americans blissfully went on a shopping spree, buying far more than
       what the country actually produced. That meant the U.S. had to import an
       increasing number of cars, toys, computers, printers, entertainment systems,
       clothing, and appliances. Paying for it proved no problem. Consumers took out
       loans from banks and handed over credit cards. Even foreigners happily lent
       money to the U.S. to finance all that spending, since it kept their own citizens
       working and economies growing.
    2. One major country that helped fuel all this American consumption was China.
       By artificially holding down the value of its own currency, the Asian giant kept
       the prices of exports well below those of most competitors. The result: All those
       sales to the U.S. earned China huge trade surpluses and a vast treasure chest
       of dollars. The Chinese central bank then took those dollars and plowed them
       back into the U.S. by buying Treasury securities. This massive inflow of money
       to the U.S. from China drove U.S. interest rates down, much to the chagrin of
       the Federal Reserve, which liked to think it has some control over the cost of
       credit.
    3. With interest rates low, Americans loaded up on debt and eschewed savings.
       They rushed out to buy homes and cars in record numbers. U.S. companies
       found the cost of borrowing so attractive that they jumped at the opportunity to
       issue long-term bonds and lock in on the lower rates.
    4. Not everyone was happy, however. Those who relied on interest income, such
       as individual investors, insurance companies, and pension funds, became
       increasingly upset with the skimpy returns they received. Low interest rates
       were great for borrowers, but not for those who relied on fixed incomes to
       achieve certain financial goals. They were hungry for investments that prom-
       ised much higher yields.
    5. U.S. financial institutions, sensing an opportunity to earn large fees, gladly
       obliged those disgruntled investors. The major investment banks proceeded
       headlong to acquire low-quality subprime mortgages because they generated
       higher interest payments. What happened next was truly staggering. These
28               Chapter 2 • A Beginner’s Guide: Understanding the Lingo




         pools of high-risk mortgage-backed assets were alchemized into murky, gener-
         ally incomprehensible securities that somehow passed muster with the major
         credit rating agencies, who classified them Triple-A safe investments. The
         imprimatur of a Triple-A rating gave large money managers and institutional
         investors (both U.S. and foreign) the green light to rush out and buy these
         securities for themselves and clients—even though they understood little about
         these investments.
      6. As public demand for these arcane but high-yielding securities surged, banks
         hurried to bundle even more of them. They urged mortgage originators to ramp
         up the pace of loans made to home buyers. The originators were happy to
         accommodate since they got paid based on the volume of loans issued. What
         followed was an absolute collapse in lending standards. Mortgages were
         handed out to virtually anyone, even borrowers with damaged credit histories.
         Applications were often approved without confirming employment or income.
         Nor did it matter whether those purchasing a home could even make a down
         payment. Simply put: If you could fog up a mirror, you qualified for a loan.
      7. The easy availability of mortgages, in turn, fired up the housing market as
         never before. Home prices leaped higher and further entrenched the view that
         real estate prices can move in only one direction: up.
      8. With credit ample and cheap, consumption of all sorts surged. Adding to the
         ebullience was that households were also feeling wealthy, since both the stock
         market and real estate jumped in value. It seemed everyone was in high spir-
         its—everyone except for a few money managers and economists who began to
         voice alarm that a dangerous housing and debt bubble was in the works.
      9. The party started to unravel after the Federal Reserve began to lift the federal
         funds rate. The benchmark rate slowly (arguably too slowly) rose from 1% in
         2003 to 5.25% in 2006. This increase made adjustable-rate mortgages more
         expensive to service. As that debt became more burdensome, the number of
         households with money problems escalated. Overextended Americans saw
         their finances deteriorate so rapidly that they went from being delinquent on
         their IOUs, to defaulting outright, to ultimately walking away from their financial
         obligations and abandoning their homes. The result: Trillions of dollars in
         mortgage-backed securities that investors blindly bought for their expected
         income suddenly stopped performing, making those investments essentially
         worthless.
     10. A disaster was also looming with the rating agencies. They came to realize that
         the models used to judge the risk and quality of mortgage-backed paper were
         horribly wrong. What followed is still mind-numbing. More than 90% of the
         Triple-A ratings given to mortgage-backed securities between 2006 and 2007
         were downgraded to junk status virtually overnight.
                              The Great Recession of 2008–2009                               29




11. The dam had now broken wide open. Investor confidence in the rating agencies, banks,
    and mortgage originators collapsed. Tens of trillions of dollars in real estate values and
    mortgage-backed securities went up in smoke. Americans were now in financial panic.
    Banks reacted by slamming shut their lending windows. Home builders froze new con-
    struction and consumers went into hibernation. The economy was now in a frightening
    free-fall.
12. The bursting of the housing and debt bubble was so violent that no corner of the globe
    was unscathed. The U.S. economic collapse engulfed Europe, Asia, and Latin America.
    Less than a decade into the new century, the world was forced to confront the most cata-
    strophic financial meltdown since the Great Depression. The steep 2008–09 economic
    downturn finally ended after Washington carried out the most aggressive monetary and
    fiscal policies in American history. Though the Great Recession technically ended the
    summer of 2009, its fallout continues to reverberate around the world.

               The Most Influential
             U.S. Economic Indicators


                        EMPLOYMENT SITUATION
    Market Sensitivity: Very high.
    What Is It: The most eagerly awaited news on the economy. Are jobs being
         created? What’s the latest unemployment rate? It has great economic and
         political significance.
    Most Current News Release on the Internet:
         http://stats.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/empsit.pdf
    Home Web Address: www.bls.gov
    Release Time: 8:30 a.m. (ET); generally announced on the first Friday of each
         month and covers the month just concluded.
    Frequency: Monthly.
    Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Department of Labor.
    Revisions: Can be major. Revisions often go back two months with each release.
         The government does benchmark changes for the establishment (or payroll)
         survey every June. Benchmark changes for the household survey are rare—
         about every ten years or so.

WHY IS IT IMPORTANT?
    This is the big one! No single economic indicator can jolt the stock and bond markets as
    much as the jobs report. The reason? To begin with, the employment news is very timely.
    It’s released just a week after the end of the month being reviewed. Second, the report is
    rich in detail about the job market and household earnings, information that can help
    forecast future economic activity. Third, let’s face it—we’re talking about the well-being
    of American workers. Wages and salaries from employment make up the main source
    of household income. The more that workers earn, the more they buy and propel the
32                   Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



     economy forward. If fewer people are working, spending drops off and business suffers.
     Because household spending accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy’s total
     output, you can see why the investment community and the Federal Reserve pay such
     close attention to the employment report.
          There is another reason it has such a hold on financial markets and policymakers.
     The job numbers often contain surprises. Experts have a difficult time trying to predict
     the unemployment figures because so little other information is out yet for that month.
          The highlight of the jobs report is, of course, the unemployment rate, which is the
     percentage of the civilian workforce that is unemployed. What do we mean by civilian
     workforce? By definition it is anyone 16 years or older who is classified as employed or
     unemployed (excluding the population in the military, prisons, mental hospitals, and nurs-
     ing homes). Economists measure monthly changes in the job market from two sources.
     One is based on the household survey, which the government conducts by telephone and
     mail interviews of households. The other is the establishment (or payroll) survey, in
     which companies are directly queried about recent changes in staffing. Together, the two
     surveys paint a sweeping picture of the labor market and, more broadly, the state of the
     economy’s health.

HOW IS IT COMPUTED?

     Household Survey
     It’s from the household survey that we derive the widely reported unemployment rate.
     Each month the government contacts 60,000 homes, a population that includes farm as
     well as non-farm workers, the self-employed, domestic helpers, and—believe it or not—
     even U.S. residents who commute to jobs in Mexico and Canada. (The point of the latter
     is that these Americans still earn money, make payments to the IRS, and are close enough
     to the U.S. to spend part of their income here.) Here’s a sample of the questions asked in
     these surveys: Are you working? Was the job full- or part-time? If you had a part-time
     job, was it because you couldn’t find suitable full-time work? If you are not working, how
     many weeks have you been unemployed? How long have you been looking for work? Did
     you make an attempt in the last four weeks to find a job?
           The response rate from households is fairly high—about 95% of those queried do
     respond. Thus, out of 60,000 households, some 57,000 come back with answers, while
     3,000 are not heard from. All the interviews are done either in the week that contains the
     12th day of each month or just days later. Based on the information received, the size of
     the civilian labor force is calculated, along with how many of these people currently have
     jobs. Then comes a simple equation: Divide the number of those over the age of 16 who
     are not working by the total number of people in the civilian labor force, and voilà!—you
     have the unemployment rate. If the size of the civilian labor force is 100 million, and 5
     million of them are out of work, the nation’s unemployment rate is 5%.
                                 Employment Situation                                    33



     Although it’s not rocket science to identify someone who is jobless, there is a bit
more confusion about who is actually included in the labor force. Normally we do not
count the military because everyone in uniform has a job, which is to protect the U.S. So
the civilian labor force is the main measure used to quantify the pool of labor available in
the economy. However, after that, the definitions get a little cloudy. Among the unem-
ployed, the government includes in its labor force only those who are actively looking for
work. What is meant by “actively looking for work”? Simply this: The individual must
have made a specific effort to find employment within the preceding four weeks. Any
jobless person who is so discouraged by the poor employment prospects that he or she is
not actively seeking employment is excluded from the labor-force count and thus is not
reflected in the main unemployment rate. (To be fair, the employment report does publish
a separate unemployment rate that includes even discouraged workers, but this little-
known figure is buried deep in the 35-page release. You’ll see precisely where in the later
section, “The Tables: Clues on What’s Ahead for the Economy.”)
     The data in the household survey can be quite valuable to anyone doing research on
demographics and marketing. It breaks down the population of those who have jobs—and
those who do not—by age, sex, ethnicity, educational achievement, and marital status.
The highest jobless rate is usually found among teenagers, both male and female. That’s
followed by blacks, Hispanics, and then whites. The lowest unemployment has tradition-
ally been married men. Another interesting pattern is the link between joblessness and
education. The unemployment rate is nearly always highest for those with less than a
high-school diploma—and then steadily drops as the level of education increases. The
workforce that consistently has the lowest unemployment rate is the group that possesses
at least a four-year college degree.
     Clearly, lots of useful information can be gleaned from the data. However, one
should bear in mind that the household jobs survey has one serious vulnerability. Its
integrity is based on the answers given by household members, and they might not always
be accurate. For example, some people may be too embarrassed to admit they are unem-
ployed and instead describe themselves as “consultants.”

Establishment Survey
The establishment survey—often referred to as the payroll survey—is considered by
many to be a better employment measure than the household survey. Consequently, it has
grabbed most of the attention of the press and money managers around the world. What’s
special about it? The information it gathers on the job market comes directly from busi-
ness establishments, not households. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) gets in touch
with 440,000 corporate and governmental work sites. These entities employ more than 50
million workers, or about one-third of total non-farm employment. The information is
obtained by both mail and telephone, and it is collected using the same midmonth sched-
ule as the household survey. Given the large number of places to contact, only 60%–70%
34                     Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



     of the responses make it back in time for the first scheduled release of the employment
     numbers. The reason for the initial low response is that small businesses are notorious for
     being late with their replies, yet these firms traditionally are the first to hire and fire work-
     ers. As more of them eventually submit their answers, the response rate climbs to the
     mid-80% range, which forms the basis of subsequent revisions in each of the next two
     months. (Incidentally, you can see what the collection rate is for a particular month here:
     www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesregrec.htm.)
           The establishment survey includes all persons on the payroll of non-farm businesses;
     nonprofit groups; and local, state, and federal government offices. Even residents of
     Mexico and Canada who travel to their jobs in the U.S. are counted. That last group
     might strike some as bizarre. Remember, however, that all the establishment survey does
     is tally the number of jobs created or lost in the U.S. business and government sectors,
     regardless of who filled those posts. The only groups excluded from the establishment
     survey are farm workers, the self-employed, and domestic help.
           What makes the establishment survey such a favorite among economists and
     investors is that it contains a veritable gold mine of data on the latest changes in employ-
     ment and income—information that can reveal much about how well the U.S. economic
     machine is working. To give you a sense of the richness of the data in the payroll num-
     bers, the government looks at more than 500 industries. Among the most important statis-
     tics from the report is the net number of new jobs formed or lost in the latest month. How
     long did the average workweek last? How much overtime was generated? What were the
     average hourly and weekly earnings in the month, and how do they compare to earlier
     periods? The establishment survey also breaks down many of these issues by geographic
     location and specific industry, so you can quickly tell which businesses and regions in the
     country are doing well and which appear to be in a slump.
           An interesting question arises at this point. Because the household and establishment
     surveys are based on two different sources, to what extent do they agree with what’s hap-
     pening in the employment market? It should come as no surprise that they occasionally
     tell conflicting stories. For instance, if the unemployment rate, a figure derived from the
     household survey, drops one month, it gives the impression that the economy is improv-
     ing and that more people are finding jobs. Yet the establishment survey might simultane-
     ously report that tens of thousands of jobs were actually lost that month.
           Why do the two measures occasionally diverge? The reason is they each probe the
     job market from different perspectives. The household survey collects data on working-
     age individuals, while the establishment survey doesn’t bother with age. It merely asks
     companies whether they hired new workers. Second, the two surveys have separate guide-
     lines. The household poll includes both farm and non-farm workers, the self-employed,
     and domestic help. In contrast, the establishment survey covers a narrower population
     segment by looking only at non-farm workers in the economy; it excludes the others.
           Another key difference between the two surveys is that the establishment report
     makes no distinction between full- and part-time work. Remember, its main focus is to
                                                                                                                             Employment Situation                                                                                               35



      report how many jobs were created. If an individual has two part-time jobs, the household
      survey counts that as one employed person, but the establishment survey classifies it as
      two jobs. Thus, if 100 new positions were created according to the establishment survey,
      this doesn’t necessarily mean that 100 people found new employment. One individual
      could be holding multiple part-time jobs. Another key difference is the treatment of those
      who are self-employed; they are counted in the household series but not in the establish-
      ment series. Thus, it is easy to see why the two reports might conflict. However, that
      doesn’t undermine their validity. Each survey has important information about the econ-
      omy that the other lacks. In any event, over the long run, both the household and the
      establishment numbers move in tandem.

                 (1) This section starts off with the latest count on the size of the “civilian noninsti-
                     tutional population.” Okay, few terms in economics can induce sleep as quickly
36          Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



     as this phrase, but bear with me. Imagine a number that represents the broadest
     number of people in the U.S. that are potentially available for work. Why
     potentially available? Clearly not every single person in the country is employ-
     able. By “available” we mean everyone 16 years of age or older—except those
     on active military duty, in prisons, mental hospitals, or some other institutional
     facility, since they are effectively unavailable to do work. The civilian noninsti-
     tutional population is thus the total pool of labor that employers can theoreti-
     cally tap.
     Below that you will see a category called the “civilian labor force,” which at
     first glance might seem identical to what was described previously, but it’s not.
     The “civilian labor force” is the sum of all who already have jobs—plus those
     unemployed who are actively searching for work. The operative term here is
     “actively,” which the government defines as individuals who have applied for a
     job at least once in the past four weeks. Those unemployed who chose not to
     seek a job during the past four weeks are no longer counted as part of the civil-
     ian labor force (though they remain part of the civilian noninstitutional popula-
     tion). To put it another way, the civilian labor force combines the number of
     those working plus all who are able and willing to work and who show it by
     seeking employment every month.
     Next is the participation rate (commonly known as the labor-force participation
     rate). Here we get a little more perspective on what is going on in the job mar-
     ket. It tells us what proportion of the entire “working age” population (which is
     civilian noninstitutional population) is actually employed or ready and able for
     work (known as the civilian labor force).
     Why is this ratio followed so closely? Simple. As a nation, we want to see as
     many people as possible on the job, or at least diligently looking for work. What
     we do not want is a situtation where the unemployed become so discouraged
     about the economy that they have simply given up looking for work. This group
     will likely cut back on spending and restrain economic growth. Nor will they
     contribute much in paying taxes.
     In a typical business cycle, the labor-force participation rate rises when the
     economy is growing robustly. The reason the rate increases is because as the
     prospect for employment and pay improves, those who stopped looking for
     work out of frustration will resume filling out applications. By doing so actively,
     they have reentered the labor force. Conversely, a falling participation rate
     points to a faltering economy. When the outlook for jobs becomes grim, more of
     the unemployed choose to stop looking for work, As a result, these individuals
     fall off the labor-force roll. They may choose to live off their savings, travel,
                        Employment Situation                                     37



return to school and learn a new trade, or enter the underground economy, all of
which reduces the labor-force participation rate.
Let’s add some historical context here. The labor-force participation rate has
been on the rise since the 1960s as more women have entered the job market.
The rate jumped from 59.1% at the start of that decade to 66.9% by 2000. But
the lingering effects of two major recessions since then have hurt the job market
enough to pull the labor-force participation rate back down to around 64%.
The household employment figure reflects the number of people who have jobs.
This measure can be a sensitive leading indicator of an economy turning up,
because it also captures the self-employed and the people they hire, something
the payroll survey doesn’t do. Both the number of self-employed and those
working for small start-up firms tend to increase at a faster rate than the rest of
the labor market in the early stages of a recovery. Thus, as a recession nears its
end, keep an eye on household employment; it may start to climb well before
the payroll statistics do.
Below that is another noteworthy metric, the employment-population ratio, and
it tells us whether the economy is generating enough new jobs for a growing
population. A high or rising employment-population ratio indicates that firms
are hiring at a pace that keeps up with the increase in population. With more of
the U.S. population at work, household incomes will rise, and that leads to
greater consumer expenditures and stronger economic growth. On the flip side,
a significant drop in the ratio can spell trouble. It means that the economy is not
producing enough jobs to absorb an ever-increasing pool of potential workers.
Not only does that hurt the unemployed, it punishes even those who are work-
ing. After all, if the supply of people seeking work swells, but hiring does not,
then employers acquire more leverage to limit pay increases.
How has the employment-population ratio performed in the past? Overall, it has
been inching higher since the end of WWII as double-income households have
become more prevalent. The ratio fluctuated around 55% from the late 1940s
to the 1960s, then marched toward 60% by the end of the 1970s, and
finally topped out at 64.7% in 2000. But within this long arc of history, the
employment-population ratio fluctuates up and down during business cycles.
Those swings allow us to draw conclusions about the path of the economy. For
instance, the severity of 2008–09 recession forced so many people out of work
that the employment-population ratio collapsed to below 60%, and it has
remained there for years. By closely monitoring changes in this ratio, we can
better foresee shifts in the job market, worker income growth, and the underly-
ing strength of the economy.

      (2) Here you’ll find the latest monthly unemployment rates for all workers, along
          with a demographic breakdown of that population. Many economists often refer
          to the unemployment rate as a lagging indicator, which means it responds
          slowly to changes in the economy. As a result, they say, one can divine little
          from it about the future. However, that’s not quite the case. By and large, the
          unemployment rate itself is of little use in forecasting an economic recovery.
          Joblessness can remain stubbornly high as long as two years after a recession
          ends because most employers are reluctant to add to their payrolls until they’re
          convinced the economy is genuinely on a solid growth path. Another reason for
          the slow rebound in job creation is that companies have made great strides in
          operating more efficiently. Thanks to the widespread use of computerized
          equipment, better inventory management, and greater foreign outsourcing of
          production, employers can more easily raise output without hiring back U.S.
          workers in the numbers they once did.
          Where the unemployment rate can serve as a leading indicator is by warning of
          an impending downturn in economic activity. Since the early 1980s, the
          increased use of sophisticated software and information technologies has
          allowed firms to respond much more quickly than in the past to changes in the
          demand for goods and services. As soon as executives detect signs of a soften-
          ing in business activity, they act faster to control costs. Because labor is the sin-
          gle largest expense for companies, layoffs are now occurring months before the
          onset of a recession. In the 1990–91 recession, the jobless rate turned higher
          more than a year before business activity turned down. When the 2001 recession
          started, the unemployment rate had bottomed out 11 months earlier. A similar
          pattern emerged prior to the the 2008–09 downturn, when the jobless rate began
          its climb seven months before the economy began to sink. Thus, this indicator
          can act as an early-warning system of an economy headed for trouble.
          One last point about the unemployment rate: Roughly 150,000 new people of
          working age enter the labor force every month simply because of the nation’s
          population growth, immigration, and students who graduate. This means that
          the economy needs to create at least as many jobs each month, on average, just
          to keep the unemployment rate from rising. Most economists seem to agree that
          to produce that many new positions month after month, the economy must over
          time expand by at least a 3%–4% annual rate. Should growth fall below that
          pace, fewer jobs will be created, and the unemployment rate will climb higher.

         (3) Want to know which economic statistic generates the most excitement in the
             stock and bond markets every month? It’s the monthly change in non-farm
             employment from the establishment data. All the figures in this section are
             derived from payroll records and represent the strongest evidence of whether the
             country is creating jobs. Many analysts evaluate the economy’s strength on the
             basis of how many net new positions have been formed. However, one has to be
             careful about jumping to conclusions. The change in the number of non-farm
             jobs created includes positions in government. To find out what is happening in
             the private business sector, one has to subtract the government’s contribution
             from total non-farm payroll. Here’s an illustration of why that could be impor-
             tant. Let’s say the establishment survey shows that the net number of non-farm
             jobs dropped by a net 50,000 workers in one month. A troubling sign for the
             economy? Not necessarily. It could be that the business community actually
40                                                       Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



                              hired 30,000 net new jobs in the month, but that was offset when the govern-
                              ment laid off 80,000 people in the same period (30,000 – 80,000 = –50,000).
                              In this example, the business community was healthy enough to add 30,000
                              workers, but that was overshadowed by cutbacks in government jobs. Thus, it’s
                              important to keep an eye on how federal, state, and local governments influence
                              overall non-farm employment.
               (4) At the bottom of Table B are the average hourly and weekly earnings for the
                   month. The value of these measures should be obvious. If worker incomes rise,
                   it bodes well for future spending. More elaborate information on hourly and
                   weekly earnings can be found in Table B-3 (not shown), which looks at pay by
                   selected industries. Rising earnings can reveal those industries that are doing
                   well and where there might be a growing scarcity of experienced workers.

               (5) Differences in hours worked is another advance indicator of future economic
                   activity. If you want to get a preview of the economy’s direction, follow the
                   changes in average hours worked in a week. It correlates very closely with over-
                   all output (GDP) and also changes in personal income. If the number of hours
                   worked increases for three consecutive months, it’s a strong sign that business
                   will soon accelerate hiring. Should the number of hours worked show a pro-
                   longed decline, expect layoffs and cutbacks in business and consumer spending.
                             Employment Situation                                      41



     The number of hours worked in manufacturing is especially sensitive to any
     shift in the public’s demand for goods. When average weekly manufacturing
     hours dips below 40, it’s often an indication that the economy is struggling,
     whereas 40.5 hours and above suggests that business activity is moving into
     higher gear. In recent history, average hours worked in manufacturing has
     ranged from a recession-level 38.5 to a robust 41 hours.
     You’ll also find in this table average weekly hours worked for nearly two dozen
     major industry groups. This information can tip off investors on the health of
     specific sectors in the economy. For example, if average weekly hours in the
     construction industry drops, it could lead to a fall in housing starts, cause higher
     unemployment among workers in real estate, and hurt other firms whose for-
     tunes are linked to home building. Indeed, anyone considering whether to buy
     or sell stocks of home-building companies should monitor these economic indi-
     cators. They can signal a change in revenues and profits with major home
     builders months before these firms release their quarterly earnings statements.
     Overtime hours are another excellent indicator of future employment and GDP
     trends. During periods of economic uncertainty, instead of hiring new workers,
     companies might ask existing employees to put in extra hours. If overtime
     increases and that pace is sustained for at least three months, firms will be under
     pressure to consider hiring again. Overtime can be quite costly to a company,
     and, let’s face it, at some point you will exhaust your present employees and
     diminish the quality of their work. Thus, rising overtime is a precursor to new
     permanent hires. Weekly manufacturing overtime normally fluctuates within a
     narrow range of between 2.1 and 3.5 hours. If it slips below 3.0 hours a week
     for a few months, layoffs might increase. A consistent reading above 3.3 over-
     time hours presages new hiring.
     One other note: The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ online database—which is
     freely available to all—drills down average weekly hours worked and overtime
     each month with much greater industry detail. Visit www.bls.gov/data/.

 (6) Figures on part-time employment tell an interesting tale that analysts often miss.
     When it’s hard to get suitable full-time work, many people have no choice but to
     accept part-time employment. This table shows the number of people in the
     non-farm economy who have accepted part-time work for economic reasons,
     which means they could not locate suitable full-time positions. A steady upward
     trend in the numbers suggests that the economy is still weak and unable to gen-
     erate enough full-time posts to satisfy job seekers. Should the number of forced
     part-time workers decline, it means that enough full-time jobs are becoming
     available to encourage part-timers to leave their posts.

                  (7) There are two keys metrics of note here. The first refers to the percentage of
                      those unemployed who are “not on temporary layoff. ” It can say a lot about the
                      severity of an economic downturn. Many industries temporarily shut down some
                      operations and lay off workers when demand for goods and services declines.
                      Once business conditions improve, many of those laid off are called back to
                                                                                                            Employment Situation                                                             43



                                     work. There are also times when companies dismiss workers who have no
                                     chance of returning. Some firms close their doors for good. Others restructure
                                     their operations or relocate factories to other countries where labor is cheaper.
                                     And then there is the churning that comes with mergers and acquisitions where
                                     workers are let go to eliminate duplicate jobs and reduce other operating costs.
                                     During periods of economic strength, the percentage of unemployed that is “not
                                     temporary” can slip to below 30%. However, that share can surge to more than
                                     50% when the economy is in serious decline, as we saw in the 2008–09 down-
                                     turn.
                                     The other statistic in this table, a particular favorite by Federal Reserve officials,
                                     is the “quit rate.” This term is jargon for what is formally listed in the table as
                                     “job leavers.” The reason this particular measure is popular with policymakers is
                                     the logic behind it. Of all those unemployed, the “job leavers” ratio represents
                                     the percentage of workers who voluntarily left their jobs to seek higher-paying
                                     opportunities. These people deliberately quit one job without immediately
                                     acquiring another, confident that they will find more lucrative employment rela-
                                     tively quickly. Normally, job leavers in this table fluctuate between 10% and
                                     15% of the unemployed. When the job leavers rate declines, it is a sign that
                                     fewer workers are willing to quit, because they see a deterioration in the job
                                     market. If the rate increases, it suggests that the economy is generating enough
                                     new jobs for workers to feel more comfortable about giving up their current
                                     posts and searching for something better.

      (8) Another very good barometer of economic activity can be found in Table A-12,
          which shows not just the size of the unemployed population, but how long
          they’ve been without jobs. In the table, the length of time unemployed ranges
          from less than 5 weeks to 27 weeks and more. A sharp increase in the number
          of persons out of work 5 weeks or less means that companies are laying off
          workers in greater numbers. Also noteworthy is the other end of the jobless
          extreme, those unemployed 27 weeks and more. That’s because by then most
          unemployment insurance benefits have expired, and this can have all sorts of
          implications for society. There is a likelihood of more crime, greater homeless-
          ness, and additional spending on public welfare programs. A falling trend in the
          duration of the unemployed is a portent that the worst of the economy’s troubles
          are over and that a recovery might be under way. (To avoid such social disloca-
          tions, Congress may appprove extending unemployment benefits for additional
          weeks.)
          One data point in this table that has been especially successful in predicting
          turning points in the economy is the number of people unemployed for “15
          weeks and over.” Without fail, this number starts to climb well before the econ-
          omy officially turns south. It generally bottoms out on average 10 months
          before the onset of a recession, but can range from 5 to 13 months. In the reces-
          sion of 2008–09, this metric began its climb a full year before the downturn
          began.
          Nearby is another important statistical clue: the average length of time of being
          jobless. During the booming 1990s, the average duration of unemployment was
          just 14 weeks; an economic slump can extend that idle period to more than 40
          weeks.
     • Table A-15 Alternative Measures of Labor Underutilization
      (9) The main unemployment rate gets a lot of play in the press. However, as men-
          tioned earlier, it excludes those who are jobless and too discouraged to even
          look anymore. The headline unemployment rate also does not factor in full-time
          workers who lost their jobs and have since grudgingly accepted part-time
          employment just to earn a few dollars. However, this table recalculates the
          unemployment rate to include these other categories (see U-5 and U-6), and the
          results can be startling. When you add other groups of discouraged workers to
          the equation, the broader unemployment rate can be as much as 7 percentage
          points above the more common headline rate.

                  (10) One of the best forward-looking clues on where the economy and certain
                       industries are headed can be found in this detailed table. One cannot overstate
                       the value of information provided here. For example, one statistic worth track-
                       ing for clues about future employment measures shifts in the hiring of tempo-
                       rary workers. Keep in mind that temp work has become an increasingly
                       important segment of the labor economy because it allows companies to oper-
                       ate with greater flexibility. More than 25% of all new positions filled by busi-
                       ness in 2010 were temporary jobs. Fifteen years earlier, temp employment
                       accounted for just 6% of all new private-sector jobs. The reason one should
                       carefully monitor the temporary workforce is that it also serves as an excellent
                       forecasting tool. Temps are the first to lose their jobs when an economy gets
                       into trouble, a trend that can begin as early as 12 months before the onset of
                       recession. Once the economy makes the important turn from recession to
                       recovery—a transition that is difficult to identify in real time—businesses will
                       prefer to employ temporary help first before taking the more expensive step of
                       permanently hiring and training new full-time employees. Once employers
                                     Employment Situation                                    47



              trust that the recovery is real, they feel more comfortable about recruiting
              permanent workers. (In addition to the Bureau of Labor Statistics monthly
              numbers on temp employment, a weekly measure can be found at the
              American Staffing Association’s Web site, www.americanstaffing.net/
              statistics/staffing_index.cfm.)
              A second great metric to follow is employment in “truck transportation.” The
              demand for truck drivers is highly sensitive to booms and busts in the eco-
              nomic cycle. If retailers and manufacturers sense that demand is slacking or
              see their inventories swelling, they will reduce new orders from their own sup-
              pliers. Since most basic commodities and finished consumer products get
              shipped to their final destination by trucks, a decline in orders will reduce
              demand for truck drivers and even lead to layoffs. On the other hand, if cus-
              tomer demand improves and inventories get too thin, new orders will rebound
              and that increases the need for truckers.
              A third useful data point is to track monthly swings in employment in the
              “child-care services” industry. As conditions in the job market improve, the
              number of working parents increases and they will make arrangements to place
              their young children with child-care centers. Many states have strict laws on
              the ratio of teachers to infants and toddlers, which means these centers will be
              obligated to hire more people to be in legal compliance. Should economic con-
              ditions deteriorate and layoffs accelerate, child-care centers will see demand
              for their service decline, and this has typically led to dismissals of caretakers.


MARKET IMPACT

    Bonds
    Traders get quite agitated when there’s a strong jobs report, especially if it’s unexpected.
    The news can portend accelerating inflation and rising interest rates, both of which are
    anathema to bondholders. Thus, be prepared for a sell-off in fixed-income securities when
    job creation is surging. How far bond prices will fall and how much yields will rise
    depends on many factors, but the most important is where the economy happens to be in
    the business cycle. If the U.S. has just managed to climb out of recession, a jump in
    employment will likely have only a modest effect on bond prices, because there’s no
    immediate danger of inflation. However, if employment accelerates when the economy is
    already operating at or near peak capacity, prepare to see a steep drop in bond prices and
    sharply higher interest rates.
         In contrast, a series of weak employment reports reflects a more sluggish economy,
    which is bullish for bond prices and means interest rates will head lower.
48                    Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



     Stocks
     News of robust employment can make equity investors positively giddy. As the number of
     people holding jobs increases and the workweek expands, employees easily slip into the
     role of consumers and spend more money. The result: Expectations rise that business
     sales and profits will pick up in the future. This can set the stage for a rally in the equity
     market. The only exception is if the economy is overheating, with interest rates and infla-
     tion turning up. The higher cost of borrowing will hurt companies and undermine stock
     prices.
          Little or no growth in employment is generally seen as bad for stocks. The worry is
     that households will be less inclined to shop. Weak sales can shrink corporate income and
     earnings, thereby reducing the incentive to own shares.

     Dollar
     Employment news can greatly influence the dollar’s value in currency markets. A vigor-
     ous jobs report could drive interest rates higher and rally stocks, which makes the dollar
     more attractive to foreign investors. They can now earn more interest income by owning
     U.S. Treasury securities and gain from higher equity values. On the other hand, an ane-
     mic jobs report softens demand for U.S. currency, because it spells trouble for American
     stocks and puts downward pressure on rates, both of which make the dollar less appealing
     to foreigners.
                                Job Openings and Labor Turnover                               49



           JOB OPENINGS AND LABOR TURNOVER
    Market Sensitivity: Low.
    What Is It The report captures the churning that takes place in the labor market.
         It publishes the the total number of new hires and layoffs in the month, as
         well as how many job openings remained in that period.
    Most Current News Release on the Internet: www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/
         jolts.pdf
    Home Web Address: www.bls.gov
    Release Time: 10:00 a.m. (ET); published about five to six weeks after the
         reference month.
    Frequency: Monthly.
    Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Department of Labor.
    Revisions: With each release, the government makes revisions to the previous
         month, though they tend to be minor. Benchmark revisions are done once a
         year, usually in March, and can go back two years.

WHY IS IT IMPORTANT?
    You might have taken notice that we began this chapter with the most anxiously awaited
    economic report of the entire month: the Employment Situation report. But even that
    major market-moving indicator lacks some vital information about what is happening on
    the job front. For example, the Employment Situation report says nothing about how
    many people were actually hired in the latest month. Nor does it tell us the number of
    jobs eliminated. Surprised? All the headline statistic in the main Employment Situation
    report (aside from the unemployment rate) is just the month-to month “change” in the
    number of people on corporate and government payrolls, which is simply the “net” differ-
    ence between the number of jobs created and the number of jobs eliminated. That’s it! So
    if the government announces that payrolls increased by 250,000 in a particular month,
    that figure merely reflects the difference in the aggregate number of new hires, less all the
    jobs that were lost. What you don’t see is the actual “gross” number of positions filled
    and eliminated.
         Why are the gross numbers so important? There is no better measure of the econ-
    omy’s health than its ability to create new positions. And the fact is that the U.S. econ-
    omy actually generates far more jobs than most of us think. How much more? This may
    surprise you. On average, 4 million to 5 million new positions are filled every single
    month in sectors like construction, manufacturing, retail, services, and the government.
    Even during the lowest point of the 2008–09 Great Recession—when the Employment
    Situation reported horrific “net” job losses month after month—another less-well-known
    economic indicator showed that more than 3.5 million new positions were filled during
50                    Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



     those same months. The problem was that an even greater number of jobs disappeared,
     which accounts for the net figure showing large losses in payrolls.
          For us to really understand what is going on in the labor market, we have to follow
     not only the Employment Situation release but also its lesser-known cousin with the awk-
     ward title of “Job Openings and Labor Turnover,” often referred to by its acronym as the
     JOLT report. What makes the JOLT report so useful to investors, business leaders, and
     policymakers is that it provides a fuller picture of the churning that occurs in the work-
     force.

HOW IS IT COMPUTED?
     The government’s Bureau of Labor Statistics breaks down the JOLT numbers into three
     main sections: job openings, hires, and separations (and the last of these is further differ-
     entiated by quits, layoffs, and discharges). To get data on each section, the BLS randomly
     contacts 16,000 non-farm business establishments each month from a universe of 9.1 mil-
     lion firms. The sample covers factories, offices, and retailers, as well as federal, state, and
     local government agencies in all 50 states. Questionnaires about job market activity are
     sent out and the answers come back by telephone, fax, e-mail, or regular mail, or via
     Web-based responses.
          Based on the survey responses, the BLS presents the data in the following format:
     Job Openings: It represents the number of jobs available on the last day of each
           month. These are positions that firms are actively recruiting from outside the
           company. It makes no difference whether the positions are full-time, part-
           time, temporary, or permanent. All are included.
     Hires: This is the total number of positions filled that entire month.
     Separations: The column aggregates the number of jobs eliminated during the
           entire month. However, there are several subgroups in this category, since
           “separations” can happen for a number of reasons. They can occur because of
           layoffs and discharges, both of which are involuntary dismissals. (Layoffs
           and discharges are often the result of mergers, downsizing, or closings, or for
           a specific cause, such as employee theft.) Quits are when employees
           voluntarily chose to terminate their employment. People might quit because
           of dissatisfaction with their work or because they are hopeful of getting better
           employment opportunities elsewhere. The final subgroup is called Other
           Separations, which covers retirements, deaths, and those who left due to
           disability.
                               Job Openings and Labor Turnover                              51



THE TABLES: CLUES ON WHAT’S AHEAD FOR THE ECONOMY
    The JOLT report is a fairly new series with data going back no further than December
    2000. Nevertheless, it has already shown some usefulness as a forecasting tool.
      • Table A Job Openings, Hires, and Total Separations by Industry,
        Seasonally Adjusted
         (1) This column reflects the total the number of job openings and their origins—the
             private sector and government. The data can serve as an important analytical
             tool for economists and investors since it tells us something about the demand
             for workers, how it changes month to month, and in what industries. In many
             ways it represents the ultimate gauge of how optimistic (or worried) employers
             are about the economic outlook, since labor is the costliest investment
             companies make.
             Where it gets interesting is that the number of job openings turns markedly
             lower well in advance of when an economy slips into recession. For example,
             job openings peaked nine months before the U.S. economy turned down in
             December 2007. This trend of hitting a high and then plummeting long before a
             recession commences also occurred in 2001, following the dot.com bust. It is a
             pattern that is likely to be repeated in future business cycles because firms are
             highly sensitive to a softening in demand for goods and services and will
             quickly pull back on job postings.
         (2) Hires: Here we have the total number of positions filled that month. It also is
             broken down by sectors. As noted previously with job openings, companies will
             typically slow the pace of hiring if they suspect that the economy is losing
             steam. Just how sensitive is this metric to downswings in business activity? The
             number of hires peaked more than a year before the beginning of the 2008–09
             recession. Although the series on “hires” hasn’t been around for very long, there
             is some empirical evidence of its value as a predictive tool.
         (3) Separations: This column contains the total count of separations, which includes
             quits, layoffs, discharges, and other reasons for separations. It tells us little
             about the economy since embedded in this category are two contradictory mes-
             sages. For example, a surge in large layoffs and discharges can certainly warn of
             rising economic problems. On the other hand, a big jump in the number of quits
             typically portends just the opposite. In a more vibrant economy, where jobs are
             more plentiful, dissatisfied workers might be more willing to quit one job and
             seek another. To better understand what is behind these separation numbers, we
             go to Tables B and C.

 (5) One can obtain a more accurate assessment on current economic conditions by
     monitoring the size of quits over time. As you can imagine, employees, no mat-
     ter how unhappy they might be at their work, are reluctant to walk away from
     their jobs and risk losing income if the labor market is awful. The propensity to
     quit is naturally much greater in a growing economy where employment oppor-
     tunities are brighter. Thus the quit numbers tend to be highest during periods of
     robust economic activity and lowest during a recession when employers are not
     in a hiring mood.
     That’s why the levels of quits and job openings often move in tandem. For
     instance, the number of workers who voluntarily left their job started to decline
     about a year before the onset of the 2008–09 recession, and did not pick up
     again until well after the recovery had started.
     One last point: Some people may wonder what the difference is between the
     quit levels in the JOLT report and the number of “job leavers” in the
     Employment Situation release. Both count how many people have opted out of
     their jobs. The answer is that they come from different sources. The monthly
     figure on “job leavers” is based on inquiries made to households, whereas the
     level of quits reflects responses from firms. Which is a more accurate reflection
     of such departures? Understandably, the quit numbers in the JOLT report por-
     tray a more reliable picture of labor-market turnover, in part because some indi-
     viduals in the household survey may be reluctant to admit to being laid off and
     prefer instead to say they left of their own accord.
