                   This table answers a fundamental question: Are American workers making a decent
                   wage? That is, are earnings rising above the cost of living? If so, consumers are
                   enjoying a rise in purchasing power, which promotes more spending and supports
                   economic growth. But if pay increases fail to keep pace with inflation on a consis-
                   tent basis, consumers will not be able to maintain their standard of living for long—
                   unless they use up more of their savings or borrow funds to help maintain their
                   consumption. The latter clearly poses long-term risks for the economy. A buildup in
                   household debt and diminshing personal savings will eventually damage consumer
                   balance sheets and force many to scale back spending. Given that household expen-
                   ditures make up 70% of economic activity, it doesn’t take a rocket scientist to see
                   that a persistent erosion in consumer purchasing power can be harmful to an
                   economy.
                   The chart provides a snapshot of worker pay and how it has grown relative to the
                   cost of living. For example, it tells us in real dollar terms what the latest average
348                    Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



           hourly and weekly earnings are for employees in the private sector, and how that has
           changed from the previous month and year-ago level. The example cited shows that
           pay levels for both have been losing ground to inflation over both time frames.
           See for yourself: In February 2011, average hourly earnings adjusted for inflation
           stood at $10.31. A year later, purchasing power dropped to $10.20—even though
           nominal wages on an hourly basis actually rose during that time from $22.88 an
           hour to $23.31 an hour. A similar disturbing trend can be seen with average real
           weekly pay. It fell from $353.49 in February 2011 to $352.05 a year later. What’s
           troubling is that this occurred despite the fact that both the number of hours worked
           and nominal wages rose over the year. The reason for the erosion in real pay is clear.
           Although workers received a 1.9% increase in nominal hourly pay and a 2.5%
           increase in weekly earnings, the cost of living during the year jumped by an even
           larger 2.9%.
           Now, let’s turn this analysis on its head. Could it be dangerous for an economy if
           consumer purchasing power rose year after year? After all, companies that conti-
           nously hand out generous raises to workers can erode profits, anger shareholders,
           and force these firms to raise the prices of their products. That would further heat up
           inflation pressures and hurt consumers.
           So can we have both rising corporate profits and an increase in household purchas-
           ing power? The answer is an unequivocal yes! The secret is to improve business pro-
           ductivity (typically by relying more on fuel-efficient technology and better
           employee training) so that firms are able to produce and sell more while keeping
           operating costs contained. That generates faster profit growth, which companies can
           then share with their employees and shareholders.
           The chart thus helps investors and economists forecast consumer expenditures, per-
           sonal bankruptcies, and corporate earnings, and might even serve as an indicator of
           future labor turmoil, especially if there is a sustained decline in real earnings.

MARKET IMPACT

      Bonds
      The real-earnings report does not have any effect on the fixed-income market because it is
      overshadowed by the market-moving CPI, which is released simultaneously.

      Stocks
      The equity market does not react to this report.

      Dollar
      The U.S. currency is not sensitive to real earnings.
                                          Yield Curve                                        349



                                   YIELD CURVE
    Market Sensitivity: Medium.
    What Is It: The range of yields on Treasury securities from short- to long-term
        maturities.
    Web Addresses: www.stockcharts.com/charts/YieldCurve.html and
        www.bloomberg.com/markets/rates/index.html
    Frequency: Always available.
    Source: Treasury markets.

WHY IS IT IMPORTANT?
    When it comes to predicting the future course of the economy, only one indicator stands
    above all others in terms of accuracy: the yield curve. No other measurement has demon-
    strated as much success in warning of upcoming turning points in business activity. The
    yield curve is a collection of yields plotted on a graph that covers the entire spectrum of
    maturities on U.S. Treasury securities. What distinguishes the yield curve from all other
    economic indicators is that historically, at least, it’s not something produced by a govern-
    ment agency or private group. Instead, it is shaped by the financial markets and is sup-
    posed to reflect the collective wisdom of investors at any moment in time on the likely
    direction of the economy and inflation.
         However, since 2008 the rules of the game have changed, hopefully temporarily. The
    Federal Reserve has chosen to intervene in the fixed-income market on a scale never seen
    before, and this has temporarily undermined the yield curve as a forecasting tool.
    Traditionally, the central bank relies on controlling short-term rates as a way to keep the
    economy and employment growing, while holding inflation in check. Longer-term rates
    were always left to the private capital markets to shape. Then came the severe recession
    of 2008–09. At first, the Fed drove short-term rates to near zero in December 2008. But
    when even that failed to revive business activity, the Fed undertook an extraordinary set
    of actions that included buying trillions of dollars in longer-term securities for its own
    balance sheet (known as quantitative easing) in an effort to bring longer-term rates down
    as well. They hoped that by dramatically lowering the cost of borrowing across the entire
    maturity spectrum, it would encourage more business and consumer spending, lift eco-
    nomic growth, and bring unemployment down more quickly.
         That experiment is still underway. But forecasters who relied on the yield curve in
    the past to predict economic trends now question its usefulness. That’s because it will
    likely take several years for the Fed to sell those securities back into the private sector
    before these rates normalize again.
         Still, the yield curve cannot be ignored because it does influence the cost of funds for
    individuals, companies, and even the government. In time, as the Fed reduces its holdings
350                    Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



      of Treasury and other long-term securities, the yield curve should regain its reputation as
      a key tool to forecast turning points in the business cycle.
           What precisely do we even mean by “yield curve”? All yield-curve graphs have the
      same characteristics. They begin on the left with the shortest maturities, which in most
      cases are 3-month Treasuries, and then progress to 6-month, 1-year, 2-, 5-, 10-, all the
      way up to 30-year bonds at the far-right side of the curve. What makes the yield curve
      such a powerful forecasting tool is its shape after you plot the yields on a graph. The
      curve can slope up gradually or steeply, appear totally flat, or be completely inverted. In a
      normal yield curve, the yield starts off low on short maturities and then gradually rises as
      the duration of the security lengthens (see Chart A). Why is this considered normal?
      Because in a typical economic expansion, investors demand a higher rate of return on
      longer-maturing Treasury debt. After all, if they decide to purchase a 10- or 30-year bond,
      investors want extra compensation in the form of a higher yield for all the unknown risks
      they face over the coming years. These risks can include inflation swings, political tur-
      moil, and war. In contrast, those investors buying short-term Treasuries have far less risk
      to worry about and thus are willing to accept a lower yield. It’s much easier to foresee
      what will happen in the next few months than to predict conditions two or three decades
      ahead.




           If a normal yield curve consists of a very gradual increase in interest rates over time,
      a steep yield curve is an extreme version of that, with yields climbing to higher levels
      much more rapidly than on a normal curve (see Chart B).
           This can occur when the economy is starting to pick up speed, causing fresh anxi-
      eties that inflation can become more problemat350ic in the near future. Such worries
      might provoke investors into selling longer-term Treasury securities, especially if they
      believe that the Federal Reserve is moving too slowly to contain emerging price
                                      Yield Curve                                         351




pressures. This will depress bond prices and drive longer-term yields higher. (On the
other hand, if the Fed is perceived to be acting quickly to preempt an outbreak of infla-
tion, investors could actually rush in to buy long-term Treasuries to lock in high yields
while bond prices are still relatively cheap. In that case, a steep yield curve will not mate-
rialize. You can see how timely Federal Reserve intervention, or lack thereof, can greatly
influence yields across the entire range of bond maturities.)
     A flat yield curve exists when both short- and long-term securities provide nearly
identical yields. It’s the first major shot across the bow, to warn that the economy is in
trouble and in danger of slipping into recession (see Chart C), a scenario that markedly
lessens the risk of inflation. Traders often buy bonds in such circumstances to capture
higher longer-term yields. The result is that bond prices appreciate and yields move down
closer to short-term rates.
352                     Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



           An inverted yield curve, in which short-term rates are materially higher than long-
      term rates, is the siren call that a recession is in the offing (see Chart D). It reflects the
      view that the Fed is keeping short-term rates too high (with money getting scarce) and
      that an economic downturn is a virtual certainty.




HOW IS IT COMPUTED?
      Plotting a yield curve is easy enough. Several major newspapers (New York Times, Wall
      Street Journal, and the Financial Times), as well as numerous financial sites on the
      Internet (see the Web locations listed at the beginning of this section), have a table listing
      the latest yields on Treasury debt. You don’t have to graph them to determine whether the
      slope of the curve is normal, flat, or inverted. Simply jot down the published yields for
      the following Treasury securities:
          • 3-month bill
          • 6-month bill
          • 1-year bill
          • 2-year note
          • 3-year note
          • 5-year note
          • 10-year note/bond
          • 30-year bond
          A normal yield curve has a spread, which is the difference in yield between the
      30-year bond and the short 3-month bill, of about 2.5 percentage points. Anything much
                                          Yield Curve                                         353



    greater than that would be considered a steep yield curve. A flat curve is one in which
    treasuries across most maturities all huddle close to the same rate, and an inverted curve
    is whenever the 3-month bill rate is higher than that of the 10- or 30-year bond. A key
    point to appreciate is that while the Federal Reserve sets yields at the shortest end of the
    curve by governing the overnight federal funds rate, it’s the market that typically
    determines all other yields.

THE TABLES: CLUES ON WHAT’S AHEAD FOR THE ECONOMY
    As stated earlier, economists and investors have been grappling with how to interpret the
    yield curve nowadays given the Fed’s involvement in the long-term market. But most
    believe that after the Fed unloads the recently purchased securities on its balance sheets,
    the yield curve will regain its use as an exceptional forecasting tool.
         So what can you learn from the yield curve once the Fed is out of the picture? After
    plotting the yields, determine the curve’s shape. If the yield curve is flat or inverted,
    chances are that the economy is, or will soon become, sluggish. Indeed, when the curve is
    inverted, the odds greatly increase that a recession is unavoidable. Just how certain can
    we be that a recession will occur? Let history be a guide. The yield curve inverted before
    each of the seven recessions from 1969 to 2007. No other indicator has shown such con-
    sistency, not even the stock market. When a recession is under way, short-term rates often
    plunge as the demand for money and credit dries up and the Federal Reserve pumps more
    funds into the economy to make borrowing even cheaper. Should the economy respond
    and start to turn up, the combination of very low yields on short-term Treasuries and a
    rebound in yields on 10- and 30-year bonds can produce a steep yield curve. It is symp-
    tomatic of an economy moving from recession to growth again. After healthy growth
    resumes, the Fed lifts short-term rates a little, and the yield curve returns to its more nor-
    mal spread of about 2.5 percentage points.
         Clearly, the yield curve has had an enviable track record of predicting turning points
    in the economy. But there are many other factors that can affect the shape of the yield
    curve too. Countries such as China, Japan, OPEC, and South Korea, which depend on
    exports for much of their economic growth, will take the surplus dollars they earn from
    their sales to the U.S. and buy Treasuries too. Such purchases enable these countries to
    better manage the value of their own currencies in foreign exchange markets. These coun-
    tries do not want to have an overly strong currency because that can harm their exports.
    To keep their currency from significantly appreciating, they will buy more U.S. govern-
    ment securities since that lifts the dollar’s value.
         Does this mean the yield curve has permanently lost its relevance? Absolutely not.
    Much depends on the magnitude of the inverted yield curve and its duration—not simply
    because it happens to be nominally inverted. One report by the Federal Reserve Bank of
    St. Louis calculated the probabilities of a recession based on the yield curve as follows: If
    the curve is normal so that the 10-year Treasury bond yield is more than 1.2 percentage
    points above the three-month bill, the chance of recession is less than 5%. When the yield
354                    Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



      curve flattens and the two have essentially the same yield, the probability of recession
      rises to 25%. If the curve ends up inverted such that the yield on 3-month bills stands 2.4
      percentage points above the 10-year bond, the odds leap to 90% that an economic down-
      turn will materialize within the next 18 months.

MARKET IMPACT

      Bonds
      Expectations of future growth and inflation by fixed-income traders determine which
      Treasury debt maturities are the most attractive to buy. Such preferences help shape the
      yield curve. However, since the outlook for economic activity and price behavior can
      change, the yield curve is constantly in a state of motion.

      Stocks
      The equity market has not taken the yield curve seriously in the past, despite its proven
      forecasting record. This is surprising because stock prices are based on expectations of
      future corporate earnings and overall business activity, both of which can be foreseen by
      the behavior of the yield curve. Indeed, studies have shown that the yield curve can serve
      as an effective market-timing strategy, yet it remains underappreciated among portfolio
      managers.

      Dollar
      Foreign-investor reaction to a flat or inverted yield curve is difficult to predict. Much
      depends on the magnitude of the inverted yield curve, which is how much higher short-
      term rates are above long-term rates, and how U.S. short-term rates stack up against those
      of other countries. It is possible that active foreign traders might choose to avoid investing
      in the U.S. because a flat or inverted yield curve is a harbinger of anemic growth, if not
      recession. That will cause the dollar to depreciate in foreign exchange markets. However,
      if the yield curve is so inverted that U.S. short-term rates are markedly higher than those
      of other nations, it can attract an influx of “hot money” from overseas as foreign investors
      seek to take advantage of the greater returns they can receive here. What do we mean by
      “hot money”? It’s fast-moving money from investors around the world who are constantly
      on the hunt for the highest possible short-term gains. The instant an investment loses its
      appeal (for example, when U.S. yields fall relative to their foreign counterparts), that hot
      money quickly leaves the borders of one country for another lucrative region of the
      world. Thus, the dollar might bounce up in value when there is an inverted yield curve,
      but its strength would be very tenuous.
           A steep yield curves suggests stronger economic growth and rising short-term rates
      in the months ahead. This will likely attract foreign investors to purchase and hold dollar-
      based financial assets.
                                Credit Manager’s Index                                  355



                OTHER NOTEWORTHY U.S.
                 ECONOMIC INDICATORS
                  CREDIT MANAGER’S INDEX
What Is It: A report that evaluates credit conditions in the business sector.
Most Current News Release on the Internet: http://web.nacm.org/cmi/cmi.asp
Release Time: 9:00 a.m. (ET); released the last business day of the month and
     covers conditions in that month.
Frequency: Monthly.
Source: National Association of Credit Management (NACM).
It is often said that credit is the lifeblood of an economy. Consumers certainly use it
extensively when they go shopping. But it’s also true that companies rely on credit when
they purchase equipment, supplies, and inventories. Sellers of these goods are willing to
extend credit to their business customers so that they will come back and buy more.
When the economy is growing, these customers typically increase purchases, often on
credit, and they tend to make timely payments. But when business conditions start to
sour, firms that financed their purchases might find it more difficult to come up with the
funds to make their scheduled payments. This begins to raise some red flags on the health
of the economy and should be a concern to investors and business leaders. One way to
keep an eye on such trends is to follow the Credit Manager’s Index.
      Every month the National Association of Credit Management, a trade group of credit
managers and collection professionals, surveys members to see whether credit conditions
are improving or deteriorating. The index focuses on credit conditions at the business-to-
business level and is based on answers to some key questions: Have credit managers
observed that their corporate customers are having a tougher time meeting their financial
obligations? Have disputes with creditors increased? Are more companies seeking bank-
ruptcy protection from creditors? Are applications for credit increasing or decreasing?
      A material change in business credit conditions can be a fairly good leading indicator
of economic turning points, and for that reason this metric has attracted more interest
among professional forecasters and investors.
356                    Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



              SMALL BUSINESS ECONOMIC TRENDS
      What Is It: An important report that tells us how confident small companies are
           about the economy, and how that will affect their own future business plans.
      Most Current News Release on the Internet: www.nfib.com/
           research-foundation/surveys/small-business-economic-trends
      Release Time: 7:30 a.m. (ET); released the second Tuesday of each month and
           contains observations made during the previous month.
      Frequency: Monthly.
      Source: National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB).
      Anyone who ignores this survey does so at great peril. Small businesses are the most
      dynamic part of the U.S. economy—so much so that they create two out of every three
      new jobs. Small businesses are also the first to ramp up production and hire workers as an
      economy emerges from recession, and the first to shut down factories and dismiss work-
      ers when business activity weakens. This tendency to react quickly and adroitly to the
      changing economic climate is why it’s important to know what the small-business com-
      munity thinks about the economic outlook. These expectations can greatly influence
      trends in employment and capital spending.
           Fortunately, the National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB) releases a
      monthly survey that takes the pulse of this business group. Among the most closely
      watched measures in this report is a table called the Small Business Optimism Index. It
      summarizes what executives think about future business conditions and why. What fol-
      lows next, however, is just as crucial. Based on their answers to key questions, we get to
      see what actions these firms say they are inclined to take in the coming months: Is it a
      good time to expand? What plans do they have about pricing? Are they going to acceler-
      ate hiring? Will they buy more inventories in the coming months? Are they going to
      increase capital expenditures? The survey even asks small-business owners to identify the
      single biggest problem they face. The NFIB, which has more than 350,000 members,
      began its survey as a quarterly report back in 1973. But as interest grew in getting more
      timely data from this important sector, it began to conduct a monthly poll, starting
      in 1986.
                                  Cass Freight Index                                    357



                       CASS FREIGHT INDEX
What Is It: A report that assesses the monthly volume and transportation costs of
     freight moving across North America.
Most Current News Release on the Internet: www.cassinfo.com/frtindex.html
Release Time: No specific time of day; released in the first week of every month
     and covers shipping activity during the preceding month.
Frequency: Monthly.
Source: Cass Information Systems, Inc.
At the very core of a functioning modern economy is the efficiency of its supply-chain
network. When we say “supply chain,” we are talking in large part about a nationwide
transportation system (trucks, planes, and railroad cars) that carries critical commodities
and finished goods to a variety of destinations that include ports, factories, wholesalers,
and retailers across North America. Monitoring the ebb and flows of traffic in the supply-
chain network can tell us a great deal about how the economy is performing. Two major
indicators that do this very well are the monthly Cass Freight Index and the Weekly
Railroad Traffic report, which is covered in the next section.
     The Cass Freight Index actually consists of two measures. The first reflects the vol-
ume of products that are shipped in a particular month. As you can imagine, when an
economy gathers more steam, factories increase orders for basic materials so that they
can speed up production. Retailers will ask suppliers to deliver more inventories to satisfy
rising consumer demand. Manufacturers are also shipping greater volumes of goods to
key U.S. ports for loading on merchant ships destined to fast-growing emerging countries.
A strong U.S. and international economy will have the entire supply-chain network busy
transporting items to where they are needed. On the other hand, a weakening global econ-
omy will do the reverse, with the volume of shipments diminishing.
     The second measure tracked by Cass Freight Index reflects changes in the cost of
shipping. Obviously, numerous factors can influence expenditures—the cost of fuel,
shortages of shipping capacity, and the competition for qualified drivers, which can drive
up wages. All these factors can have an inflationary impact on the U.S. economy, espe-
cially at the producer price level. The report itself is put together by Cass Information
Systems, which processes more than $20 billion in freight transactions annually on behalf
of 350 large shippers. Both the freight volume and the expenditure data are derived
directly from these operations.
358                    Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



              WEEKLY RAILROAD TRAFFIC (FREIGHT)
      What Is It: A timely report on the volume and types of commodities carried by
           rail freight cars across the country.
      Most Current News Release on the Internet:
           www.aar.org/NewsAndEvents/Freight-Rail-Traffic.aspx
      Release Time: Between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m. (ET); released every Thursday and
           covers freight rail traffic in the preceding week.
      Frequency: Weekly.
      Source: Association of American Railroads.
      Very few economic reports possess the qualities of being both exceptionally timely and
      sensitive to shifts in the business cycle. One that does have such attributes is the weekly
      report on freight traffic in North America by the Association of American Railroads
      (AAR). This release, formally called Weekly Railroad Traffic, contains separate tables on
      freight rail traffic in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico and is based on reporting by 13 major
      railroads. The data is presented in a well-organized format. First, it looks at traffic in
      terms of carloads, which can be in boxcars, hoppers, or tank cars, and they often carry
      raw or intermediate-level commodities. These goods generally make their way to facto-
      ries. The AAR tracks some 20 different commodities that these carloads transport, includ-
      ing lumber, petroleum products, coal, chemicals, and metals. An economy on the rebound
      will increase demand for these items, and that shows up in the number of freight cars car-
      rying such commodities during the preceding week.
           The report also monitors rail traffic of intermodal units. Intermodals are structures
      physically placed on rail cars that can be carried on different modes of transportation. For
      instance, a flatbed rail car can carry a trailer (with wheels) that eventually gets hooked to
      a truck at a final destination. Another intermodal unit is an enclosed container (which has
      no wheels) that is lifted off a rail car and moved onto either a cargo ship or a flatbed
      truck. Intermodal units generally contain finished goods and get delivered to warehouses
      or retail stores. Both carloads and intermodal units move in tandem with the business
      cycle. However, some commodities carried on carloads—such as lumber or chemicals—
      can serve as leading indicators of economic activity, which is why the Weekly Railroad
      Traffic reports can be useful in understanding where the economy stands in the business
      cycle.
                               Architecture Billings Index                             359



             ARCHITECTURE BILLINGS INDEX
What Is It: The index measures demand for architectural services and can
     foreshadow commercial construction activity.
Most Current News Release on the Internet:
     www.aia.org/practicing/economics/
Release Time: 8:30–9:00 a.m. (ET); released the third or fourth Wednesday of
     each month and covers activity in the preceding month.
Frequency: Monthly.
Source: American Institute of Architects.
One of the largest sectors in the U.S. economy is commercial construction. This $800
billion industry accounts for about 5% of GDP and employs millions of workers. It is also
an excellent barometer of overall confidence in the U.S. economy. Indeed, when the econ-
omy is on a sustained growth path, spending on commercial construction typically accel-
erates faster than most other sectors. But then when doubts arise about the economic
outlook, few sectors fall faster. Given the planning and capital costs involved in nonresi-
dential construction, confidence in the economic outlook is an essential prerequisite for
these projects to proceed. To help fellow architects better assess the climate for commer-
cial construction activity, the American Institute of Architects (AIA) in 1995 began to
poll a number of architecture firms for the latest trends in billing for services. Today,
some 300 architecture companies participate in a monthly survey to report whether
billings have increased, decreased, or remained the same in the preceding month. The
AIA then computes a diffusion index in which a score of more than 50 indicates that most
firms are seeing an increase in activity, whereas a score below 50 means that respondents
have seen a decline in business.
     One reason the Architecture Billings Index has grown in popularity among forecast-
ers is that an increase in billings can foreshadow a pickup in construction activity within
the next 9 to 12 months. A construction boom will not only benefit architects but also
increase the demand for construction material, equipment, and labor, all of which help
fuel more economic activity.
360                    Chapter 3 • The Most Influential U.S. Economic Indicators



                S&P/CASE-SHILLER U.S. NATIONAL
                      HOME PRICE INDEX
      What Is It: Many people believe this series is the most reliable in calculating
           changes in the price of single-family homes.
      Most Current News Release on the Internet:
           www.homeprice.standardandpoors.com
      Release Time: 9:00 a.m. (ET); released the last Tuesday of each month and
           contains home price changes of two months earlier.
      Frequency: Monthly.
      Source: Standard & Poor’s, Fiserv, and MacroMarkets LLC.
      Although there are a dozen or so indicators that track changes in home prices around the
      country, many analysts point to the S&P/Case-Shiller series as perhaps the most accurate
      of the bunch. Two economics professors and a private money manager—Robert Shiller of
      Yale, Karl Case at Wellesley, and Allen Weiss—collaborated in the 1980s and 1990s to
      come up with a more precise calculation of how much home prices change over time.
      Shiller, in particular, has earned a well-deserved reputation for being far ahead of the
      curve in spotting dangerous excesses in the valuation of assets, particularly in real estate
      and stock prices. The S&P/Case-Shiller Home Price Index represents a continuation of
      the excellent research he and his colleagues have done. What makes this series stand out
      is that it tracks only homes that sold at least twice during a covered period. By following
      price changes for the same single-family home over time, one can get a more reliable
      measure of how real estate values change. In contrast, prices published by the Commerce
      Department and by Realtors can be skewed because they can include a different mix of
      homes sold each month.
           Case-Shiller indexes are calculated monthly, and are based on a three-month moving
      average. For example, January’s data will be shaped by sales that have also taken place in
      November and December. Keep in mind that Case-Shiller does not report prices by giving
      a dollar figure. Instead, an index is compiled from which percent changes are calculated
      to show how prices have moved from the preceding month and from a year-ago level. The
      year-over-year figure is judged to be more meaningful. Its two most popular metropolitan
      groupings are the 10- and 20-city composite price indexes.
                      CHAPTER 4


International Economic Indicators:
   Why Are They So Important?

 U.S. economic indicators help us understand what is happening in the domestic economy.
 However, to be a successful investor or an effective corporate leader in today’s highly
 integrated global economy also requires knowledge of what is going on beyond U.S. bor-
 ders. A CEO who wants to sell products overseas or an investor who seeks to achieve
 higher returns on stocks and bonds should be familiar with indicators that gauge the
 health of foreign economies.
      Why place so much emphasis on the international business climate? One reason is
 that most of the growth in the world economy is taking place within the emerging coun-
 tries, not the large industrial nations. Secondly, the performance of U.S. corporate profits,
 stocks and bonds, and the dollar is affected by foreign developments more than ever
 before. A recession in Europe harms not only companies on that continent, but many
 U.S.-based firms as well. Close to half of the earnings of S&P 500 firms originate from
 sales outside the U.S. Companies in the energy and technology sectors, for example, gen-
 erate more than half of their revenues abroad. Moreover, it just makes good business
 sense to be aware of new opportunities that become available in markets outside the U.S.
 By diversifying into Europe, Asia, and Latin America, one is no longer bound to the eco-
 nomic swings of just one country. Indeed, there is much fertile territory to choose from in
 other markets. Equity investors, for example, can pick from more than 45,000 public
 companies that are listed on world stock exchanges, 75% of which are outside the U.S.
      To be sure, there are additional risks to consider when investing overseas. One of the
 biggest is adverse movements in currencies. If you own securities or other assets in
 another country and their currency climbs in value against the dollar, great! The overall
 return on that investment gets an added lift because it is more valuable in dollar terms.
 However, should that currency happen to weaken relative to the dollar, the investment
 will be less valuable or perhaps even turn into a loss when it is sold and the proceeds are
 converted back to dollars. Thus, shifts in foreign exchange values can potentially make or
 break a foreign investment.
362             Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?



           Given the risks currencies pose, wouldn’t it make more sense to simply shy away
      from international markets? Absolutely not. There is nothing inherently mysterious about
      the movement of the dollar, euro, yen, British pound, or any of the other major free-
      floating currencies in the foreign exchange markets, for ultimately, the long-term value of
      a currency is determined by a country’s economic fundamentals. Is the economy grow-
      ing? Does inflation remain under control? Are consumers and businesses confident about
      the future of their economy? Are government fiscal policies responsible? Does the coun-
      try have adequate savings for investments? Is its international trade account in reasonable
      balance? These are the issues that have the greatest influence in determining currency val-
      ues. Sure, exchange rates might fluctuate in the short term due to differences in interest
      rates or from occasional uncertainties born of economic or political instability. But, by
      and large, the true value of a currency is based on the economic soundness and vitality of
      the country behind it.
           Another criticism heard about entering foreign markets is that the benefits of global
      diversification have been oversold. According to this argument, markets overseas increas-
      ingly appear to march in lock step with those in the U.S., so why bother investing else-
      where, where the risks are greater? It is true that during periods of crises, whether they be
      economic, political, or military, markets around the world tend to move in unison.
      However, such moments of high global tension are uncommon, and these parallel move-
      ments in the value of assets around the world are usually very brief—a matter of days or
      weeks at most. Generally, foreign financial markets tend to pursue their own direction.
      Canada’s stock market historically has a 65% correlation with the U.S.; for the U.K. it is
      50%. German equities have a 55% correlation, and Japan has less than 20% relationship.
      Case in point: Just look at the best and worst performers by national stock markets over
      the last several years, as shown in Table 4.1.

Table 4.1 Ranking Stock Market Performance by Country (Based on Local Currencies)

          As you can see, the U.S. is listed just once among the top performers in recent years.
      The point of this table is to underscore the importance of keeping an open mind about
         Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?       363



investing in foreign markets, especially in the emerging countries. While no one can pre-
dict with certainty which economies and financial markets will outperform others, one
outcome is assured. Over the next generation we will see hundreds of millions of new
middle-class consumers emerge in the developing countries, and they will be the main
driving force in the global economy for decades to come. There should thus be no dispute
that the virtues of diversifying investments abroad remain as valid as ever.
     This chapter is designed to take you to the next level, which is to identify the foreign
indicators that provide the best read on current and future global economic conditions.
Certain barometers of economic activity abroad should be followed with the same regu-
larity and scrutiny as U.S. indicators so that investors and business managers have a
chance of achieving success in international markets. The problem, much like with the
U.S., is that there is a vast amount of foreign economic data in the public domain.
Hundreds of countries churn out thousands of statistics on a regular basis. Even if you
narrowed down the number of countries worth monitoring to two dozen, the task of fol-
lowing all the indicators that flow from these nations can still be overwhelming. Besides
the sheer variety of international statistics, many of them are difficult to locate when
needed. Often they are defined and computed differently than indicators in the U.S. and
can vary greatly in quality. A large number are not even presented in English.
     This section tries to overcome these problems. In the following pages, we select the
most important foreign economic indicators for closer study. They represent the three
major non-U.S. markets in the world: Europe, Asia, and Latin America. As is the case
with U.S. economic statistics, these foreign indicators are released to the public on a pre-
determined schedule. Calendars of international economic releases can be found on the
Web sites listed at the start of Chapter 6, “Best Web Sites for International Economic
Indicators.” All the international indicators presented here are available on the Internet.
They originate from either official government or private association Web sites, are free
to the public, and can be viewed in English.
     Finally, note that international data is presented in different formats. Many countries
use commas instead of decimal points and a period or a space instead of a comma to indi-
cate the thousands place. For example, the U.S. and Germany both represent numbers
using decimal points and commas, but sometimes the symbols are interchanged (2,325.77
versus 2.325,77). At other times, Germany (and France) might use a space as the digit-
grouping symbol (2 325,77).
     International dates are also displayed differently around the world. In the U.S., the
month precedes the day; Europeans mostly use day-month-year, whereas Asian cultures
use year-month-day. Why isn’t there a single standard for all countries now that world
economic and financial systems are so closely integrated? Tradition and politics. These
two hurdles are difficult to overcome. Those favoring a uniform worldwide format will
have a long wait. In the meantime, one has little choice but to get used to these local cus-
toms and move on.

                 GERMAN INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION
      What Is It: Industrial output in Europe’s largest economy.
      Most Current News Release on the Internet:
           www.destatis.de/EN/Homepage.html
      Home Web Address: www.destatis.de
      Release Time: 11:00 a.m. (Continental time); released the first or second week of
           the month and refers to activity two months earlier (so March data describes
           production in January).
      Frequency: Monthly.
      Source: Federal Statistics Office, Germany (Statistisches Bundesamt,
           Deutschland).
      Revisions: Revisions can occur with each release and cover the two preceding
           months.
      We begin with Germany, Europe’s richest and most populous country. Its output alone
      accounts for a third of everything produced in the Eurozone, the name given to the region
      of 17 countries* that use the euro currency. Germany thus holds enormous sway over the
      Continent’s well being. It is the country all of Europe relies on to help solve the region’s
      economic woes. However, Germany’s influence also extends far beyond Europe. It is the
      world’s fifth-largest economy and the second-biggest exporter. It is also a key trading
      partner of the U.S. and an important investor. Trade between the two countries now
      exceeds $140 billion. Outside of Europe, the U.S. is Germany’s biggest economic partner.
      Indeed, German companies account for about 800,000 jobs in the U.S., and American
      firms have established roughly 500,000 positions in Germany.
           Given the dominance of its economy over Europe and the fact that it is a key player
      in the world as well, Germany’s industrial production figure ranks at the top of the must-
      watch list. Though industrial output accounts for less than a quarter of the country’s GDP,
      this indicator has been correlated with GDP changes in the Eurozone overall. Thus,
      investors and business executives who want to spot early signs of strength or weakness in
      Europe will find Germany’s industrial production index a good leading indicator.

             GERMAN IFO BUSINESS CLIMATE INDEX
      What Is It: German business leaders assess the current and future economic
           climate.
      Most Current News Release on the Internet: www.cesifo-
           group.de/portal/page/portal/ifoHome/a-winfo
      Home Web Address: www.cesifo-group.de/portal/page/portal/ifoHome
      Release Time: 10:30 a.m. (Continental time); published the third or fourth week
           of the survey month.
      Frequency: Monthly.
      Source: The CESifo Group.
      Revisions: Tend to be rare. Periodic revisions occur as a result of changes in
           seasonal adjustment factors.
      Among the most anticipated economic statistics to come out in Europe every month is
      Germany’s IFO Business Climate Index. From the time it was launched in 1949, this
      series has proven to be a very good leading indicator of how the German economy and,
      more broadly, the European economy will perform in the weeks ahead. Of course, a simi-
      lar claim was made of the industrial production index. But what makes the IFO report
      such a sensitive one for investors is the timeliness of the data—the results are released the
      same month the survey is taken.
           At the start of every month, the Institute questions more than 7,000 German business
      leaders and senior managers covering the manufacturing, construction, wholesale, and
      retailing industries. All are asked to appraise Germany’s current business situation
      (good/satisfactory/poor), as well as their expectations over the next six months (more
      favorable/unchanged/more unfavorable). Their answers form the basis of the total
      Business Climate Index and its two principal subcomponents: the Present Situations
      Index, which assesses current economic conditions, and the Expectations Index, where
      those queried are asked to forecast what the business environment might be a half year
      later.
           Of the three index results, European financial markets tune in more closely to the
      expectations series. History has shown that movements in the Expectations Index tend to
      lead changes in the Eurozone’s industrial production by about two or three months. Thus,
      if the IFO expectations gauge turns up, odds are it will shortly be followed by an acceler-
      ation in factory output in Germany and perhaps much of Europe as well.
           After the reunification of Germany, the IFO Institute initially published two separate
      business climate readings—one for eastern Germany and the other for western Germany.
      However, in 2004, the decision was made to combine the two sets of data to represent
      business activity in Germany as a whole. Economists at the IFO believed that the business
      cycles for these two regions had by now largely converged, even though they were still
                                   German IFO Business Climate Index                           367



      operating at different output levels. Thus, the IFO Business Climate Index now publishes
      a united German series for its headline index. Those who still want to see separate per-
      formance data for western and eastern Germany can do so by searching the more detailed
      IFO database on its Web sites.
           Finally, it is interesting to note that the IFO Business Climate Index appears to have a
      close correlation with the U.S.’s own Institute for Supply Management (ISM) manufac-
      turing report. Over the years, a persistent rise in the ISM numbers has, after a six-month
      lag, been accompanied by an increase in the German IFO expectations index. Given the
      size and importance of the American economy in the world, this probably is not all that
      surprising. This linkage between the two surveys is yet another illustration of how inter-
      woven the international economy has become.




Source: IFO Institute for Economic Research, used with permission.
368            Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?



            GERMAN CONSUMER PRICE INDEX (CPI)
      What Is It: The main price inflation gauge for Europe’s largest economy.
      News Release on the Internet: www.destatis.de (click “English”)
      Home Web Address: www.destatis.de
      Release Time: 7:00 a.m. (Continental time); the preliminary CPI is published
           around the 25th of every month. Final figures are released two weeks later.
      Frequency: Monthly.
      Source: Federal Statistics Office Germany (Statistisches Bundesamt
           Deutschland).
      Revisions: Monthly report on the CPI might contain revisions for earlier months.
      As the economic pillar of Europe, Germany can serve as the engine of growth for the
      Continent, or it can be responsible for dragging down the region. Which role Germany
      ultimately plays depends on many factors, but none more important than the performance
      of its own inflation. Germany’s CPI can have a powerful impact on the economies of
      other European nations and on the policies of the European Central Bank (ECB), which
      sets short-term interest rates for all 17 countries using the euro currency.*
           If German inflation is increasing at a troubling rate, the ECB will likely raise interest
      rates even if the other neighboring economies show their inflation to be relatively tame.
      On the other extreme, should Germany get caught up in a deflationary spiral in which
      prices are consistently falling, the ECB is expected to jump in and lower rates to preempt
      a similar collapse in prices from spreading to the rest of the continent.
           Germany’s CPI has been on the radar screen of investors worldwide for decades. Its
      high profile can be traced to the country’s oath to avoid at all costs a repetition of the cat-
      astrophic hyperinflation it experienced in the 1920s, when prices for essentials like bread
      and milk jumped several hundred percent every day, making its national currency essen-
      tially worthless. That painful memory led the Bundesbank (Germany’s central bank) after
      World War II to set in stone a tough, inflexible, anti-inflationary policy, and it has never
      veered from that stance. For decades the Bundesbank showed zero tolerance for the
      slightest whiff of inflation beyond 2% a year. It made no difference whether the economy
      was weak or unemployment was sky-high. The primary mandate of the central bank was
      to keep inflation close to zero and protect Germany’s currency, the deutsche mark, at all
      costs, even if it meant lifting and holding rates at painfully high levels. Although
      Germany’s dogged defense against inflation contributed to years of chronically high job-
      lessness, it also made its currency one of the most revered in the world.


             * See the earlier section on German industrial production for the names of 17 countries shar-
               ing the euro.
                          German Consumer Price Index (CPI)                             369



      During talks to establish the euro in the 1990s, Germany made clear to European
negotiators that it would join the currency union only if the new European Central Bank
agreed to pursue the same tough anti-inflationary position shown by the Bundesbank.
German officials wanted the euro to have the kind of respectability in global currency
markets that the mark had. That would mean keeping interest-rate decisions for Eurozone
nations out of the hands of politicians. Even today, Germany’s influence on the ECB is
palpable; Europe’s central bank firmly toes the line that it will not permit inflation to
exceed the 2% range for the Eurozone.
      This does not mean the ECB as a matter of policy will disregard all other economic
stresses in the region. During the gravest moments of the Eurozone’s sovereign debt cri-
sis, for example, the central bank surprised many by showing a more pragmatic side. As
the danger of sovereign defaults in Europe grew in 2011, many feared that the fallout
would ultimately lead to a catastrophic collapse of the Eurozone. But the ECB boldly
dropped short-term rates to a historic low and lent out massive amounts of low-cost funds
to nervous European banks—and did so even though inflation in the region remained
above the central bank’s target.
      Let’s take a closer look at Germany’s inflation measure itself. The CPI measures the
average change in prices for all goods and services bought by households for the purpose
of consumption. In the middle of the month, about 560 price collectors, working out of
state government offices across Germany, collect prices on a basket of 750 specific goods
and services. Overall, approximately 400,000 prices are obtained each month, including
taxes (value-added and excise taxes) and price discounts (such as sales or rebates). The
Federal Statistics Office (FSO) then compiles these price changes for six key German
states (Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Brandenburg, Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia, and
Saxony) and announces the much-awaited preliminary inflation rate for the month, along
with the latest 12-month change.
      Another virtue of the German CPI is how current it is. The government puts out a
provisional estimate of inflation around the third or fourth week of the month. A final
CPI is published two weeks later, between the 10th and 15th of the following month. It is
the provisional figures, though, that traders in the financial markets react to most because
the difference between the preliminary German CPI and the revised numbers tends to be
negligible.
      Without meaning to complicate this subject, it is necessary to know that the FSO also
calculates another version of Germany’s inflation every month, which is in the same press
release. Why produce two CPI versions? The reason for the second version is to follow a
standardized European formula for measuring the CPI. This allows business leaders,
investors, and economists to more accurately compare Germany’s inflation rates with
those of its neighboring countries. Called the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices
(HICP), and dubbed “hiccup,” it is the official inflation computation for the 27 member
states of the European Union (EU), plus Norway, Iceland, and Switzerland. When all is
370            Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?



      said and done, though, the difference between the national definition of the German CPI
      and the Harmonized CPI for Germany is not significant.

    ZEW INDICATOR OF ECONOMIC SENTIMENT
What Is It: A popular, near-real-time survey of confidence from top investors in
     Germany.
Most Current News Release on the Internet: www.zew.de/en/publikationen/
     Konjunkturerwartungen/Konjunkturerwartungen.php3
Home Web Address: www.zew.de/en//index.php3
Release Time: 11:00 a.m. (local time); released midmonth and covers survey
     results of the same month.
Frequency: Monthly.
Source: ZEW Centre for European Economic Research.
This final indicator from Germany came into being two decades ago and has two impres-
sive features going for it. First, the report is released in the same month the survey covers,
which makes it quite timely, and second, it has a fairly impressive track record as a lead-
ing economic indicator of the German economy. Here’s how it is designed. The ZEW
Centre for European Economic Research solicits responses from around 300 investors
and analysts during the first two weeks of every month on what they expect economic
conditions in Germany will be in six months. More specifically, they are asked about their
outlook for inflation, short- and medium-term interest rates, the yield on ten-year German
government bonds, stock market indexes, currencies, the profitability of firms, and even
forecasts on the price of oil.
     But here’s one other aspect about this release that makes it so worthwhile to follow.
These financial experts are told to assess future conditions not only in Germany, but also
for the Eurozone, the United States, Japan, Great Britain, France, and Italy. The questions
are all on a single page, which allows for faster processing of the responses and a quicker
turnaround time for the results to be released to the public. Thus, each month we get a
near-real-time appraisal from European investors on where they see certain key world
economies heading.
     The calculation used to compute the index is quite direct. The index represents the
difference between the percentage share of analysts who are optimistic and the share of
analysts who are pessimistic. So if 55% of participants expect the German economic situ-
ation to improve within the next six months, 20% expect no change, and 25% expect the
economic situation to deteriorate, the ZEW Indicator of Economic Sentiment would have
an index value of plus 30. A positive number thus means that the share of optimists out-
weighs the share of pessimists, and vice versa.
     This report is closely followed by European investors and economists and is known
to be highly correlated with the IFO Business Climate Index mentioned earlier. That
makes it a major market-mover in Europe.

             JAPAN INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION
What Is It: Measures the change in monthly industrial output.
Most Current News Release on the Internet: www.meti.go.jp/english/statistics
Home Web Address: www.meti.go.jp/english
Release Time: 8:50 a.m. (local time); a preliminary report is released in the final
     week of the next month. A revised report is published another two to three
     weeks later. (For example, data on October is announced during the last week
     in November, to be followed by another report on revisions in mid-
     December.)
Frequency: Monthly.
Source: Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry (METI).
Revisions: Monthly and annual revisions are frequent and can be substantial.
Few modern economies have faced as many predicaments as Japan. After achieving one
of the highest growth rates in the world from the 1960s to the 1980s, Japan has since
struggled to regain its footing. A severe stock market and real estate crash brought
repeated recessions in the 1990s, with many labeling those years as Japan’s lost decade.
To get the country back on its feet, Japan’s central bank lowered short-term rates to near
zero, and the government put through a series of financial and regulatory reforms to
encourage more borrowing, spending, and investment. The results were encouraging.
After several false starts earlier this decade, the economy appeared to be on the mend.
But then came the devastating earthquake in 2011, which shook the nation to its core. The
violent movement of the earth unleashed a horrific tsunami and brought the country close
to a nuclear catastrophe with the meltdown of its Fukushima reactor. While the economy
will ultimately benefit from the billions being poured in to rebuild the affected area,
Japan’s woes are far from over. It still faces an aging population, high public debt, an
excessive reliance on exports for economic growth, and has to rely on imports to supply
virtually all the fuel it needs.
      Despite all these challenges, Japan’s importance to the international economy and its
influence in global capital markets remains largely undiminished. It holds title as the
biggest exporter of investment capital in the world and owns an economy exceeded in
size only by the U.S. and China. It sells $850 billion worth of goods and services a year
to other nations. Japanese companies are also powerful competitors in several major
industries, such as autos, electronics, and robotics. Moreover, the yen continues to stand
alongside the U.S. dollar and the euro as one of the three most important currencies. For
all these reasons, global investors and business leaders, especially those in the U.S.,
closely monitor Japan’s economic health.
      Also looming large for Americans is the fact that Japan is the second-largest foreign
owner of U.S. Treasury securities. As a result, Japanese banks, insurance companies, and
374            Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?



      government agencies have helped fund the U.S. government budget for years, lending
      hundreds of billions of dollars. However, this is also a cause for concern. Serious finan-
      cial and economic problems in Japan could easily spill over into the U.S. Investors in
      Japan, for example, might decide to purchase less U.S. Treasury debt or even sell some of
      their holdings in dollar-based financial assets. They can also choose to manipulate the
      value of the yen to help export sales. Indeed, few countries in the world intervene in the
      currency markets as much as Japan.
            Given the ability of Japan’s economy to affect asset values in world capital markets
      and to sway currency markets, foreign investors know they have to stay informed about
      the soundness of the economy. That means paying particularly close attention to its indus-
      trial production, which many experts consider to be one of the best barometers of busi-
      ness activity in Japan. Analysts prefer to monitor industrial output over GDP because the
      former comes out sooner, responds faster to changes in the business climate, and is rich
      with information on the country’s manufacturing and mining industries. In fact, Japan’s
      industrial production release is more comprehensive in its coverage of the economy than
      its U.S. counterpart. Case in point: Japan’s monthly production report even includes fore-
      casts of how key manufacturers are expected to perform in the next two months.
            In view of all the attention paid to Japanese manufacturers, it might be surprising to
      learn that manufacturing activity makes up less than a quarter of the GDP. But this figure
      is very misleading because the actual impact that manufacturers have on the economy is
      much greater. For example, exports represent a primary engine of growth for Japan.
      Strong foreign demand for cars, digital cameras, HDTVs, and computer accessories feeds
      right through to the domestic economy by stimulating capital investment spending,
      employment, and overall output.
            Japan started measuring industrial production in 1953, and it now includes virtually
      all privately owned companies in mining and manufacturing, regardless of size. The main
      task of the industrial production series is to compute monthly changes in output for 536
      items. Figures are also given for the actual quantity of goods being produced, shipped,
      and kept in inventory for many commodities.
            The initial release, called the Preliminary Report on Indices of Industrial Production,
      is published a month after the period being covered ends. A revised release is issued
      about three weeks later. One can access the industrial production report in two ways.
      There is a summary report on the Web (www.meti.go.jp/english/statistics/). Inside that
      report is another link where you can download the complete 72-page release as a PDF
      file. The tables shown in this section come from that detailed report. Data is presented in
      both English and Japanese and is well organized, with years and dates on the right.
      Figures are seasonally adjusted with an index base of 100 that is currently tied to the year
      2005. Keep in mind that revisions are frequent and can be very large.
                           Japan Industrial Production                                375



• Mining and Manufacturing: Industrial Production
  (1) This is the summary page of the industrial production report. It provides the lat-
      est monthly and annual changes in output. (The release shows it was up 0.8%
      for the month of October and up 3.6% over the year.) A black triangle near a
      number indicates a decline. Other pages in the report (not included here) pro-
      vide additional details on the strength and weakness of individual sectors.
• Mining and Manufacturing: Shipments
  (2) Industrial shipments represent actual sales and can be used to determine
      demand. If shipments are increasing, this will likely lead to further increases in
      production in the months ahead. Should shipments begin to slacken, it will
      cause inventory levels to swell and discourage future production. (In the table,
      shipments climbed 1.2% for the month and 5.1% over the year.)
• Mining and Manufacturing: Inventories and Inventory Ratios
  (3) This section sheds light on the supply-and-demand pressures in the industrial
      sector. A rise in the inventory index reflects the quantity of goods produced that
      remains unsold. The inventory ratio index is similar to the inventory-sales ratio
      in the U.S., except that it uses an index rather than months of supply on hand.
      The ratio, which represents inventories divided by shipments, can be a leading
      indicator of future industrial output.
• Survey of Production Forecast
  (4) Included in the industrial production release is a projection of what output is
      expected to be the next two months. It’s a useful addition because the numbers
      provide a sense of where the economy might be heading. (The data in this table
      shows that production is predicted to increase 3.1% in November but drop 0.9%
      in December.) This page also breaks down the main components of production,
      enabling you to identify which sectors will help raise output and which will
      drag it down. (For example, General Machinery output is predicted to surge
      18.7% in November and fall 8.8% in December.) However, you should view this
      forecast table with some skepticism. Projections historically tend to be on the
      high side.

                          JAPAN’S TANKAN SURVEY
      What Is It: A widely anticipated report on business confidence in Japan.
      Most Current News Release on the Internet:
           www.boj.or.jp/en/statistics/tk/index.htm/
      Home Web Address: www.boj.or.jp/en/
      Release Time: 8:50 a.m. (local time); results are published at the start of April,
           July, and October, and in mid-December.
      Frequency: Quarterly.
      Source: Bank of Japan.
      Revisions: Statistical corrections are rare. Revisions merely reflect changes in
           confidence and plans from one quarter to the next.
      Aside from the U.S., Japan has arguably the most extensive collection of economic indi-
      cators in the world, much of it in English and freely available on the Web. Perhaps that’s
      to be expected from the third-largest economy (after the United States and China).
      Among the reports Japan churns out is the Tankan survey, which has gained worldwide
      recognition for its sweeping coverage, forward-looking features, and quick release to the
      public. International investors and managers of multinational companies look to the
      Tankan report for the latest reading on the state of the Japanese economy and its forecasts
      of business activity in the months ahead. What gives this survey extra credibility is the
      agency behind it. The Tankan survey is produced by the Bank of Japan, the country’s cen-
      tral bank, and its results can be used to formulate future monetary policy. As a result, this
      closely watched quarterly report has a history of moving stock prices and currencies.
           Often described as a business confidence survey, the Tankan survey is really much
      more than that. Indeed, this report offers more insight into what the business community
      is thinking than does any comparable U.S. economic indicator. If you want to know about
      Japanese plans for future capital investments, employment, or expectations of pricing
      power, and predictions of where the yen will likely be valued in the future, this release
      covers all this and a lot more.
           The survey itself is conducted quarterly by the Research and Statistics Department at
      the Bank of Japan. Questionnaires are sent out the last month of every quarter—March,
      June, September, and December—to about 11,000 firms. These companies are differenti-
      ated by their size—large (on average 22% of the sample), medium (27%), and small
      (51%)—and by industry type, with more going to nonmanufacturers (60%) than to manu-
      facturing (40%). Amazingly, the response rate of these surveys tends to be better than
      98%!
                                Japan’s Tankan Survey                                  379



    Respondents are asked to answer eight broad questions:
 1. Business conditions (favorable or unfavorable?)
 2. Supply-and-demand conditions (excessive demand or excessive supply?), inventories
    (excessive or insufficient?), and prices (rising or falling?)
 3. Sales and current profits (% change)
 4. Fixed investment at non-financial institutions (% change)
 5. Fixed investments at financial institutions (%)
 6. Employment (excessive employment or insufficient?)
 7. Corporate finance (easy or tight monetary conditions?)
 8. Business conditions at financial institutions (favorable or unfavorable?)
     Of the eight topics, five seek qualitative assessments that require a judgment call
(topics 1, 2, 6, 7, and 8). After these responses are collected, a diffusion index is com-
puted by simply calculating the percentage of businesses reporting a negative tone and
subtracting it from the percentage indicating a positive tone. The remaining three ques-
tions (3, 4, and 5) ask for quantitative changes in percentage terms regarding recent per-
formance, as well as expectations about how this will change in the future.
     The following sections highlight a few of the most useful tables in the Tankan survey.
   • Business Conditions for Large Manufacturers
     (1) Manufacturing is one of the main engines of growth in Japan because it includes
         the country’s vital export industry. In this table, we see confidence improved in
         December (actual result) to a net 11, representing a 10-percentage-point gain in
         confidence from September’s survey. However, these same manufacturers have
         predicted a slight deterioration in conditions in the next few months, because the
         diffusion index on the forecast dropped back to 8.
         Aside from the summary number at the top of the table, confidence levels are
         also broken down into broad industry categories such as motor vehicles and
         industrial machinery.
   • Business Conditions for Nonmanufacturers
     (2) This section is a good measure of the strength of consumer demand in Japan.
         Large nonmanufacturers conduct most of their business in the country and do
         not benefit much from strong export growth. One can look at the headline figure
         to get an idea of domestic demand, as well as how specific sectors are doing.
         For example, retailers noted that conditions barely improved over the past quar-
         ter, moving from –14 to –13. Note, however, that more of them appeared opti-
         mistic about conditions in the subsequent three months because the forecast
         index rose to –5.

 (4) How the yen is valued in relation to other currencies can make all the difference

     This table represents the best guess by major Japanese manufacturers as to what

     for the year as a whole. Indeed, there is a correlation between how cheap the
     yen is expected to be and the level of business confidence by large manufactur-
     ers. The lower the yen’s value in foreign exchange markets, the more upbeat
     manufacturers become because it effectively drops the price of Japanese-made
     goods abroad.
• Prices by Large Enterprises
 (5) Companies that can raise prices generally achieve higher earnings and hire more
     workers. However, there are times when businesses find it difficult to lift prices.
     Either competition prevents them from doing so, or the economy is undergoing
     a deflationary spiral in which prices are under continuous pressure to fall. The
     latter has been a serious problem with Japan throughout the 1990s and beyond.
     This index represents the percentage of companies saying their prices had risen
     versus those that lowered prices. The numbers show that slightly more firms in
     the latest survey have raised prices. The index for large manufacturers inched up
     from –23 in September to –21 in the December survey. But that might prove to
     be just a brief reprieve because the expectations index fell back to –24.
• Fixed Investment

     marker of confidence that companies have about future business activity. Here

         As rich as the Tankan survey is with information on the private business sector in
    Japan, there are two cautionary points to consider. First, since the powerful Bank of Japan

    on monetary policy by the central bank. Therefore, respondents could be tempted to
    shape their answers in a way that can result in a favorable interest-rate policy. Second, a
    large part of the survey depends on forecasts, which might turn out to be inaccurate.
    Aside from these caveats, the Tankan survey is viewed by the international investment
    community as a valuable and well-regarded economic report.

      Most Current News Release on the Internet:

      Home Web Address: www.ntc-research.com/
