      The popularity of the U.S. purchasing manager surveys has spawned a bunch of similar
      measures in other countries. The U.S. Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) for manufactur-
      ing, produced by the Institute for Supply Management, is one of the hottest economic
      indicators out every month. It has demonstrated a solid track record of anticipating turn-
      ing points in the business cycle and for being way ahead of the curve in detecting a
      buildup of inflation pressures. Indeed, it is so highly regarded by investors, economists,
      and policymakers that many other nations have developed their own PMI series in recent
      years, all basically modeled after the U.S. The purchasing managers survey was launched
      in the U.K. in 1991, followed by Germany (1996), France (1998), Japan (2002), and
      China (2005). All told, purchasing manager indexes are available for more than two
      dozen countries and they can tell us quite a lot about activity in these individual countries
      and, together, the strength of the global economy.
           Collecting all this data is a London-based firm called Markit Economics. When it
      comes to global economic intelligence, few companies can match the vast array of finan-
      cial, business, and economic information it provides. For the Purchasing Managers series,
      the firm gathers data from more than 16,000 companies across more than 20 countries
      every month, and seeks to track activity in manufacturing, services, retail, and construc-
      tion sectors. In addition to producing a PMI for the Eurozone, Markit Economics teamed
      up with HSBC, another global financial services company, to come up with a PMI series
      of China, and with J.P. Morgan for a global PMI—and the results for all can be seen on
      Markit Economics’ Web site.
               Manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) by Country and Region            385




        We’ll focus on three of the most eagerly awaited international PMI manufacturing
    reports: one on the Eurozone, a Global index, and one on China.

EUROZONE MANUFACTURING PMI
    Established in 1997, the Eurozone Manufacturing PMI is one of the first composite indi-
    cators out every month on conditions in eight countries: Germany, France, Spain, Italy,
    Ireland, Greece, Austria, and the Netherlands. They represent 92% of all manufacturing
    activity in the euro currency area. The report is based on responses from 3,000 purchasing
    executives. Markit Economics collects the data from the individual national surveys as
    well and then recomputes a regional index for each of the major questions asked. Finally,
    an overall headline index is calculated to reflect total manufacturing activity in the region.
         At the heart of the surveys are questions to purchasing managers that cover six key
    themes:
386           Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?



      1. Is the level of new orders received by your company higher than, the same as, or lower
         than one month ago?
         This question addresses the issue of demand in the economy. If demand for goods
         increases, it will drive up manufacturing output.
      2. Is the level of output in your company higher than, the same as, or lower than one
         month ago?
         The focus here is on whether there’s been a shift in production to higher levels because
         of new orders.
      3. Is the stock of items purchased by your company higher than, the same as, or lower
         than one month ago?
         For manufacturers to keep their production lines running smoothly, they need to have
         an ample supply of raw materials on hand. But as output accelerates, supplies typically
         diminish and purchasing managers need to reorder more stock. Thus, the purchase of
         new items is linked to the pace of production.
      4. Are supplier delivery times experienced by your company longer than, the same as, or
         shorter than one month ago?
         Just because a purchasing manager places an order to replenish its stock of raw mate-
         rials doesn’t necessarily mean it will arrive overnight. Suppliers generally can ship raw
         materials to manufacturers faster in a slow economy. In a booming economy, however,
         when lots of orders for raw materials are coming in at the same time, suppliers can’t
         instantly satisfy all the demand. Bottlenecks emerge, and even suppliers have their own
         production constraints. As a result, shipments to manufacturers slow and this leads to
         delays in deliveries. Thus, longer lead times between orders and deliveries of raw mate-
         rials are a sign of faster economic growth, whereas rapid deliveries suggest slower
         business activity.
      5. Is the average input price experienced by your company higher than, the same as, or
         lower than one month ago?
         It should come as no surprise that when many manufacturers increase orders simulta-
         neously, demand for raw materials can outstrip supplies. This places upward pressure
         on factory input prices.
      6. Is the level of employment at your company higher than, the same as, or lower than one
         month ago?
         There is a link between employment in manufacturing and production. Greater demand
         for new orders often leads to more employment. However, over time, the relationship
         between jobs and output turns more tenuous. Given the high cost of labor, manufac-
         turers might try investing more in improving productivity than in expanding their
         workforce to raise output. Thus, production could increase at a faster pace than job
         growth in the long run.
               Manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) by Country and Region        387



         The results are presented in the form of a diffusion index. A reading of less than 50
    indicates a contraction of activity, above 50 points to an expansion, and an index of
    exactly 50 says that no change has occurred.
         In addition, an aggregate index is computed using a weighted average of five (of the
    six) queries above. It is based on the following formula: The new orders response is given
    a 30% weight, output 25%, employment 20%, supplier delivery times 15%, and stocks of
    items purchased 10%. You’ll notice that the PMI index on prices is left out of the equa-
    tion. Though input prices are a very good leading indicator of producer price inflation,
    changes in prices can occur for many reasons that have nothing to do with the business
    cycle. Strikes, currency movements, restrictions in supplies by foreign producers, and
    bizarre weather all influence input prices of raw materials regardless of the pace of eco-
    nomic activity. As a result, the change in price data is excluded from the total survey
    index.

GLOBAL MANUFACTURING PMI
    First released in October 2003, the Global PMI series wants to be considered a gauge of
    world manufacturing trends. It functions the same way as the Eurozone purchasing man-
    agers report, except that it includes a larger sample. J.P. Morgan and Markit Economics
    have worked together to collect responses from 9,000 purchasing managers in 30 coun-
    tries that collectively represent 86% of the world’s total manufacturing output. Again,
    what makes this report so useful are the questions asked; they inquire about real activity
    (specifically, output, new orders, input prices, and employment) and do not solicit per-
    sonal or subjective views. A reading of 50 indicates no change from the preceding month.
    Below 50 is a sign of contraction, and above 50 points to an expansion.
         I should add that in addition to a manufacturing index, there are also separate
    releases on activity in the service sector for the Eurozone and Global PMIs. Services
    account for a predominant share of the GDP in most modern industrial economies.
    Although that’s not the case with the large emerging countries, even they have seen serv-
    ices grab an increasingly larger share of their economies in recent years.
         So which PMI series—manufacturing or services—can better foreshadow economic
    turning points? For Europe the answer appears to be the purchasing managers index for
    services since there is evidence that this index has a better correlation with changes in
    GDP than the manufacturing PMI. But if you are trying to anticipate shifts in “global”
    economic activity, most investors still track the global manufacturing PMI. The reason is
    that for the U.S. and in most developing countries, the goods-producing sector tends to
    respond more immediately to changes in demand than services. However, given the
    dynamic growth in services worldwide, you can expect the Global PMI Services Index to
    match the influence of its manufacturing cousin over the next decade.

CHINA MANUFACTURING PMI
      Thanks to the combined efforts of HSBC and Markit Economics, we are now able to get
      more precise economic data on China, and it couldn’t come at a more important time. For
      the past three decades, China has been the fastest-growing economy on the planet. What’s
      truly mind-boggling is that it took just five years for the country to cruise past the United
      Kingdom, Germany, and Japan to become the second-largest economy in the world.
      Some have argued that China is now within a generation of exceeding even the U.S. If so,
      it wouldn’t be unprecedented. For much of recorded history, China had the largest econ-
      omy in the world, before it flamed out in the 19th century and most of the 20th century as
      civil wars, conflicts with Japan, and the reign of Mao Zedong damaged the country. Since
      1978, however, it has bounced back in spectacular fashion, and China is once again a pal-
      pable force in the global economy.
           Today, investors, economists, business leaders, and policymakers spend as much time
      wondering about the economic outlook in China as they do the U.S. and Europe. One
      important metric that helps analysts understand the underlying momentum driving the
      Chinese economy is the HSBC/Markit Economics monthly report on China’s Purchasing
      Manager’s Manufacturing Activity Index. This survey is based on replies from purchas-
      ing managers representing more than 400 small, medium, and large manufacturers in
      China, including both private and state-owned enterprises. HSBC then releases two PMI
      reports on China each month. The first is the “Flash” report, based on 85% to 90% of the
      survey responses. That is followed a week later with a “Final” PMI. Both publish diffu-
      sion indexes on manufacturing output, new orders, new export orders, employment, back-
      logs of work, prices, inventory of finished goods, quantity of purchases, and delivery
      times.
           (The HSBC/Markit Economics PMI report on China should not be confused with
      China’s own purchasing managers series, which often comes out on the same day. The
      country’s own National Bureau of Statistics and the China Federation of Logistics &
      Purchasing use a larger sample and a different methodology than HSBC to come up with
      its own purchasing managers index. What happens when the two purchasing managers
      reports on manufacturing head in different directions? In such circumstances, we have to
      put greater weight on HSBC/Markit Economics series because their methodology is more
      transparent than the government’s. In fact, no one quite knows what goes into the govern-
      ment survey and that opaqueness raises some skepticism about its validity.)
           The surprisingly quick acceptance by the public of purchasing manager surveys as a
      whole comes at a time when there is much frustration with the slow release of official
      economic statistics by governments. Some, like the GDP, are published 60 to 70 days
      after the quarter ends. Another complaint about official data is that countries use different
      methods to come up with the same indicators. This complicates efforts to make compar-
      isons between economies. Finally, figures can be of such poor quality that they are fre-
      quently followed by substantial revisions.

           In contrast, the Eurozone, Global, and Chinese PMI series overseen by Markit
      Economics employ the same basic methodology with all the countries, so comparisons
      are much easier to make. What’s more, revisions to the data are extremely rare. This is
      not to say that these international surveys are without shortcomings. One problem is that
      they make no effort to quantify the degree of change. For instance, if a large number of
      purchasing managers say they witnessed just a modest improvement in activity in the lat-
      est month, that alone is enough to propel the index sharply higher. Nevertheless, the pur-
      chasing manager series has gained a large following with investors and has on numerous
      occasions moved markets with the release of its data.

OECD COMPOSITE LEADING INDICATORS (CLI)
What Is It: A statistical guide to forecast business activity in the world’s largest
     economies.
Most Current News Release on the Internet: www.oecd.org/std/cli
Home Web Address: www.oecd.org
Release Time: Noon (Continental time); data is released in the second week of
     the month and refers to activity two months earlier. (For example, January’s
     release reports leading indicators for November.)
Frequency: Monthly.
Source: Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
Revisions: The previous month’s data is frequently revised with each new
     release.
Investors and policymakers love to follow leading economic indicators because of their
look-ahead qualities. They are supposed to predict short-term movements in an economy
by using measures that are highly sensitive to upcoming changes in business conditions.
The U.S. has its own set of domestic leading economic indicators from the Conference
Board, a business research group in New York (see the section “Index of Leading
Economic Indicators [LEI]” in Chapter 3, “The Most Influential U.S. Economic
Indicators”). On a global scale, however, the best-known and most closely studied equiva-
lent is the OECD’s own Composite Leading Indicators (CLI). This Paris-based interna-
tional organization computes a leading economic indicator index for 29 member countries
and 6 major nonmember nations. The regional zones covered are the Total OECD area,
the Eurozone currency area, the G7 countries, and the Big Five Asian economies (see
Table 4.2). Although some countries produce their own in-house leading indicators, it’s
the OECD’s own indexes that make the big headlines and draw the greatest interest
among money managers and policymakers.
      Using economic data from its member countries, the OECD calculates CLI indexes
designed to forecast what’s ahead for industrial production in the OECD nations and
regions. Why industrial production and not the more broad-based GDP? First, industrial
output is seen as an effective proxy for GDP because, historically, turning points in indus-
trial production have coincided with the overall economy. Second, using industrial pro-
duction as a reference point is more practical because that data comes out every month,
whereas the GDP is available only quarterly.

           Now for the obvious question: Does the OECD’s CLI really work? Is it reliable in
      picking up signals of a pending slowdown or rebound in economic growth? Here we get
      one of those “Yes, but…” answers. To begin with, anticipating turning points is not easy.
      Signs are often elusive or ambiguous. Second, much depends on the quality of the under-
      lying data from national governments, not to mention the judgment calls involved in set-
      ting up the leading indicator models and the assumptions behind them. By and large, the
      OECD’s leading indicator series gets a thumbs-up from economists and large investors.
      Even central bankers review the CLI data when setting interest-rate policy for the euro
      currency zone. Over the years, the CLI has proven to be an effective early-warning sys-
      tem, able to identify peaks and troughs in economic activity some nine months in
      advance.
           The OECD has been publishing the CLI since 1981, and the methodology is fairly
      straightforward. Financial indicators with a reputation for being ahead of the economic
      curve are chosen as components of this indicator. Among the most common national
      components used by the OECD to calculate the CLI are stock prices, building permits,
      monetary data, and production orders. Indeed, more than 100 components are employed
      to come up with a monthly (Table 1) “Composite Leading Indicators.”
           (1) If there are three consecutive months of year-over-year negative or positive
               changes, chances are the economy or a region is within 6 to 12 months of reach-
               ing a high or low point in economic activity.
           (2) The OECD also provides a brief assessment on whether recent trends in the
               Composite Leading Indicators signal an upcoming turning point in the business
               cycle.

      What Is It: Measures the monthly change in China’s industrial output.

      Let’s begin with stating the obvious. China’s blazing economic progress the past three
      decades has been unmatched by any country in modern history. From the catastrophic
      social and economic failures of the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976), China has managed
      to bounce back with such ferocity that it seems the planet’s center of economic gravity
      has shifted to the Far East. After all, no country produces more steel, cement, mobile
      phones, color TVs, and cars. Indeed, one can argue that given China’s manufacturing
      capabilities and its massive financial resources, it is difficult to justify calling China an
      “emerging economy.” The country has assembled several world-class industries, includ-
      ing aviation, autos, and computers. Its technological prowess is already a cut above that
      of most industrial countries. China owns the second-fastest supercomputer, built the
      fastest passenger train in the world, and has launched an astronaut into space, only the
      third country to do so. All of this has helped catapult the People’s Republic of China to
      become the world’s second-largest economy. These are hardly the attributes of a strug-
      gling emerging country. China, of course, argues that it has still not “emerged” enough to
      be classified an industrial economy because its per capita GDP (the size of its economy
      divided by population) remains among the lowest in the world, which is true. But one fact
      is beyond dispute: China looms large as a genuine economic superpower.
           Certainly as a consumer market, China offers opportunities limited only by imagina-
      tion. Here is a nation of 1.3 billion people and growing, including a labor force of more
      than 800 million, all eager to work and spend money. Consumer demand has been climb-
      ing steadily the past two decades as households have been driven to improve their stan-
      dard of living. That can be seen not only by their larger and better-furnished residences,
      but also in the use of high-tech consumer products. Despite government controls, China’s
      Internet population is now the largest in the world, with more than 500 million citizens
      surfing the Web (as of 2012), an exponential jump from just 620,000 users 15 years
      earlier.
                               China Industrial Production                                397



     The broader question is, what intentions do China’s top political leaders have for the
country? Government officials talk about fortifying their “socialist market economy,” a
strange brew in which socialist ideals can be met in conjunction with a more liberal,
open, and capitalistic economy. What is so interesting is that this bizarre mix has so far
worked quite well for China. Its economy has grown nearly 10% a year the past two
decades. Moreover, Chinese policymakers have successfully steered the country away
from several global economic storms, including the Asian financial crisis and the Russian
debt default in the late 1990s, the collapse of the dot.com bubble (2000–01), and the
2008–09 global economic downturn. They avoided these pitfalls largely because the gov-
ernment quickly ordered policies that were designed to protect their economy from out-
side shocks. Case in point: While other major economies were in free-fall during the
2008–09 recession, the Chinese government quickly implemented a nearly $600 billion
stimulus program. The result? At a time when most other economies were shrinking,
China’s GDP grew an annual average of more than 7% from 2008 to 2010.
     Impressive? Yes. But the absence of any parliamentary debate on economic policy is
not a practice to emulate. For there are also signs that Communist China is starting to
bump up against the limits of Capitalist China. For instance, even though the country has
grown much wealthier in recent years, the inequality in income among its population is
getting wider and may incite more social unrest. All that spectacular growth has simply
not translated into greater prosperity for the vast majority of its people. Indeed, inequality
in China is growing at a faster rate than in Brazil or India, according to the World Bank.
     To reduce the income gap and address other economic problems, there is evidence
that China is creeping toward a more market-oriented economy. More than half of the
business sector is now in private hands. Concrete steps are being taken to shift economic
decision making away from a centralized, command-style system. What’s more, China’s
ascension to the World Trade Organization in 2003 is supposed to bring its economic and
currency policies more in line with world standards, but that process has been agonizingly
slow so far. In the meantime, China’s rapid expansion and massive consumer market con-
tinue to attract international investors and multinational business leaders. Large foreign
investment bankers see in China a rich source of new clients as an increasing number of
companies there are being permitted to access global capital markets to raise funds.
Credit ratings firms, such as Standard & Poor’s, Fitch, and Moody’s, are also charging
into China to assess the creditworthiness of its companies and government agencies.
China itself has become a major player in the international community. With a war chest
of more than $3 trillion in foreign exchange reserves, by far the largest in the world
thanks to its cumulative trade surpluses, China is in a position to buy huge chunks of for-
eign government bonds, stocks, real estate, and other types of assets.
     And yet, even with all the attributes that make it an economic superpower, the coun-
try has at least one noticeable problem: Many foreigners suspect that China puts out dubi-
ous statistics about its economy. This poses a genuine problem for foreign firms and
investors who need to appraise the country’s current and future well-being. Longtime
398            Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?



      observers have complained that China’s economic numbers are less accurate than those of
      other industrialized countries, even going so far as to say that key officials “cook the
      books” to impress foreign investors and lenders. In recent years analysts have charged
      that China was overestimating its GDP growth to lure foreign capital. At other times,
      there were accusations that Chinese statisticians were intentionally underestimating
      growth to create the impression that the economy was not overheating.
           Behind these statistical problems lies an antiquated data collection system, one that
      can be traced back to the old command economy days. During the 1950s and 1960s,
      Communist party headquarters relied extensively on production reports from local man-
      agers, who would often lie about output figures to curry favor with party leaders. Small-
      town Communist officials were often promoted based on the economic performance in
      their region, so it was in their best interest to embellish the figures. Thus, to some extent,
      the problem was not so much at the headquarters level in Beijing, but with the field
      reports from local and municipal managers. Today, China’s National Bureau of Statistics
      (NBS) still gathers output figures much the same way as before, though the fabrication is
      believed to be less widespread. Nevertheless, China still has no independent method in
      place to check the veracity of local production reports.
           This doesn’t mean Beijing officials are sitting idle. They are well aware that without
      a trustworthy source of economic information, it will be hard for foreigners to make
      investment decisions or for Chinese leaders to carry out the right fiscal and monetary
      policies. The NBS has been working in earnest to upgrade the quality of its economic
      reports. Among the modifications introduced recently was a change in the manner in
      which statistics are collected. For example, Chinese officials decided in March 2005 that
      data collectors should be placed under the authority of the NBS. This can help redress
      many of the statistical inaccuracies that originate from local municipalities. Second, the
      government revamped how GDP is computed. This redesign was critical. The traditional
      statistical reporting method failed to capture the growth under way in the expanding serv-
      ice industries, such as real estate agents, business consultants, and companies offering
      communication services. To correct this shortcoming, the government conducted its first-
      ever nationwide economic census in 2004, and the results were startling. At the end of
      2005, China announced that its economy was actually much larger than previously
      thought. Virtually all of the upward revision came from services, which turned out to rep-
      resent more than 40% of all economic activity, nearly 10 percentage points higher than its
      prerevision share. It was fresh evidence that China’s economy is becoming more diversi-
      fied than first believed.
           In 2011, the NBS took another important step to bring its economic statistics more in
      line with Western standards. The agency began to publish GDP growth rates on a quar-
      terly basis, rather than just note how output has changed from the same quarter a year
      ago. China has also gotten much tougher with government employees who abuse the eco-
      nomic data. When two officials sought to enrich themselves by leaking the numbers on
      GDP, retail sales, and consumer price inflation before their scheduled release, prosecutors
      cracked down hard by giving them stiff prison sentences.

         Another way that China has moved to bring its economic reports up to global stan-
    dards was to make the data more accessible to everyone in the world. Here we see an
    earnest attempt by China’s NBS to construct a user-friendly Web site with detailed infor-
    mation on economic output, inflation, and other measures of performance, and much of it
    in English. By going to the home page of the National Bureau of Statistics
    (www.stats.gov.cn/english), one can begin to stay on top of the country’s key economic
    data.
         (1) Release Calendar: The NBS makes available an economic calendar for key eco-
             nomic statistics.
         (2) Statistical Data: High-frequency economic indicators—such as retail sales,
             industrial production, consumer prices, and GDP—can be found based on their
             schedule of releases.
400            Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?



           (3) Press Releases: A very good start to get the latest economic data can be found
               here. View a sample of a press release on industrial production below.
            (4) NBS’s Press Release on Industrial production: Topping the list of perhaps the
                best and most timely measures of economic performance in China is its indus-
                trial production series. It measures changes in output for the industrial sector of
                the economy, which includes manufacturing, mining, and utilities. Industrial
                Production is a key metric for economic forecasting and can anticipate changes
                in inflation. For example, high levels of industrial production can heat up pric-
                ing pressures and ultimately force the government to clamp down on output by
                raising interest rates or curbing bank loan growth, or both. Every month, the
                NBS issues a seven-page report on industrial output that contains the latest offi-
                cial analysis, a detailed table of how key sectors have performed, and graphics
                that illustrate how production and its components performed over the past 12
                months.
           Anyone who wants to monitor the latest trends in China’s economy should familiar-
      ize themselves with China’s NBS online Web site. Having said that, we have to return to
      one big underlying concern. China does not do itself any favors by keeping secret the
      methodology of how it computes many of these economic indicators. To bolster public
      confidence in its economic data, the government needs to be much more transparent on
      how the data is gathered, what weights are being given to different sectoral groups, and
      what calculations are used to compute these statistics.

INDIA: INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION AND INFLATION
What Is It: The two main indicators are among the most relevant in monitoring
    India’s economy.
Most Current News Release on the Internet: http://mospi.nic.in/Mospi_New/
     site/inner.aspx?status=3&menu_id=84
Home Web Address: http://mospi.nic.in/Mospi_New/site/Home.aspx
Release Date:
     Industrial Production: Second week of the month.
     The “New” Consumer Price Index: Third week of the month.
     Wholesale Price Index: Second week of the month.
Frequency: Monthly.
Source: Central Statistical Organization, Ministry of Statistics & Programme
     Implementation.
India’s emergence as an economic power often gets overshadowed by its giant neighbor
to the east. That’s unfortunate. Not only is India coming into its own, but many believe
that the country will eventually surpass China in both population and total output by
2050. What’s so compelling about India is that its stunning growth since the early 1990s
can be traced to a strategy that sets it apart from other developing countries in the region.
From the beginning, India cleverly positioned itself so that it did not have to compete
head-to-head with China and the other Asian countries. Indeed, what India did was defy
the textbook path toward economic development. Virtually all emerging countries in the
20th century used their cheap labor and whatever capital they could scrape together to
build up their manufacturing or agricultural capabilities. Exports and construction became
the key drivers of economic growth for these countries.
     However, India followed a strikingly different road by capitalizing on its own unique
comparative advantage. India, like China, enjoys a large population (1.2 billion versus 1.3
billion for China), but the characteristics of these two groups differ in important respects.
India’s labor force is younger, is more traveled, and speaks English. Given these attrib-
utes, business leaders concluded that economic success would more likely come from
services, and less from manufacturing. As a result, the country now offers a panoply of
important services to the world, including banking, insurance, engineering, media, soft-
ware, business outsourcing, medical diagnostics, telecommunications, and film entertain-
ment. (India’s film industry, for example, is the biggest in the world, in both the number
of movies produced and the number of tickets sold.)
     India has thus bucked the trend by choosing to rely more on services than manufac-
turing or natural resources as a means to achieve healthy economic growth. This decision
has propelled its $1.7 trillion economy to be the third largest in Asia and eleventh largest
in the world. Moreover, India’s blistering growth rate has led to an escalation in wages
404            Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?



      among service-sector employees, and especially for skilled workers. This has enhanced
      family income and stimulated domestic demand. To give you a sense of how rapidly the
      country is changing, back in 1991, India had a total of five million telephone lines in the
      country. Now it is adding five million new phone connections each month!
           One of the burning questions investors ask is whether India’s economy can continue
      to race ahead as it has. Can it conceivably even overtake China in total output? The
      answer to both questions is yes, though the latter is probably a few decades away. India’s
      prospects look bright for several reasons. First, the country has undertaken substantial
      political and economic reforms the past two decades. It has rejected socialism, opened its
      economy to more imports, deregulated industries, allowed the rupee to float more freely,
      and reduced barriers to trade.
           Second, India’s leaders also realized that the country cannot depend on services for-
      ever to keep its economy robust. And they certainly do not want the country to be viewed
      as simply a back-office operation for American companies that consists mainly of call
      centers, customer help lines, and computer programmers. So fresh domestic and foreign
      capital has also been directed to establish a sophisticated manufacturing industry, one that
      utilizes state-of-the-art technology and embraces the latest techniques of just-in-time
      inventory. The results have so far been impressive. India’s annual growth in manufactur-
      ing is now accelerating at about the same pace as services. All told, India’s service indus-
      try accounts for 63% of the GDP; the industrial sector contributes 20%; and agriculture,
      which was the backbone of its economy shortly after the country gained independence,
      has now taken a back seat in the 21st century and contributes only 17% to the GDP.
           Given the country’s extraordinary economic accomplishments, international investors
      are making the inevitable comparisons with China. Though China’s economy is four
      times the size of India’s, the question often asked is, who really will have the edge in the
      years ahead?
           Certainly both countries have enormous potential to grow and prosper. But there are
      some important differences between them that might shape their economic destiny:
          • Cultural purists may yell and scream about it, but the fact remains that English is
            the language of international business. In this respect, India has a big advantage
            over China. The medium of communication in India’s colleges and universities is
            English. Indeed, India is the world’s largest English-speaking country. The ability
            of workers and management to effectively communicate with customers and
            investors around the world is critically important to attract foreign capital and to
            find new markets for Indian-made products.
          • India has a long tradition of democracy and known for having a transparent legal
            system. In contrast, China, while it has made some strides to decentralize its econ-
            omy and allow more local autonomy, is still run by an autocratic Communist lead-
            ership. Its legal system is far from a model of transparency, and its courts are
            subject to political pressure. What’s more, social unrest has increased in China,
                          India: Industrial Production and Inflation                       405



      especially in rural farm areas. Such strife is symptomatic of a country that is strug-
      gling to pursue two inherently conflicting goals: allowing more market capitalism
      in the economy, and preserving its Communist political heritage and the ideologies
      that stem from it. The social tension that comes from pursuing two incongruous
      objectives is not expected to subside anytime soon. With so much uncertainty
      about China’s long-term stability, investors may place greater faith in the future of
      a more open India.
    • No economy can prosper unless it has a healthy banking system that can finance
      consumer and business activity. India’s banking system, though much smaller than
      China’s in terms of assets, is far healthier and better capitalized. India’s loans, for
      example, are priced according to risk, so interest rates tend to be higher than those
      in China. China has historically chosen to keep rates artificially low, in part
      because policymakers want to keep its currency (the yuan) undervalued. However,
      that has also allowed Chinese banks to issue such artificially low-interest-rate loans
      to domestic borrowers, including failing state-owned enterprises, and that raises
      questions about the future viability of such loans. Keep in mind that China has had
      to bail out its banks more than once in the past decade. Meanwhile, India’s regula-
      tors appear determined to keep its banks financially sound from the outset. They
      demand high capital requirements for lenders and make sure that these institutions
      have sufficient provisions set aside against bad loans.
    • Unlike India, China faces a serious demographic squeeze in coming years. The
      Communist country has implemented a “one family, one child” policy, and Chinese
      households have mostly adhered to it. As a result, birthrates and family sizes have
      been shrinking since 1980. No such policy exists in India; consequently, its popula-
      tion is much younger on average and more dynamic. Experts predict that India will
      end up with a larger population than China in the next five years or so. If that trend
      materializes, it will have profound implications for both countries. As China strug-
      gles to service an aging workforce that draws down national savings, India will
      enjoy a more youthful, active, and prosperous labor force. This can help catapult
      India’s economy past China by midcentury.
      But it’s not all smooth sailing for India. If the economy is ever to meet its full poten-
tial, India will first have to address some serious internal shortcomings. One is the critical
need to upgrade its creaking infrastructure. India’s road transportation system is in dismal
shape. Highways make up less than 5% of its road network, and this makes it tough to
transport goods around the country. In addition, there is a critical shortage of lodging
facilities, and this has hurt both tourism and foreign business travel in the country. There
were only 140,000 hotel rooms in all of India in 2011, whereas China had more than ten
times as many. Also in dire need of expansion are India’s ports. There are not enough of
them to handle all the merchant ships that arrive and leave with goods, and this has ham-
pered the flow of both imports and exports. Government officials also have to beef up the
406            Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?



      nation’s power-generating system. Right now India does not have enough plants to satisfy
      the electrical demands of a fast-growing economy. Blackouts are not uncommon, even in
      Bangalore, where the country’s high-tech computer and software industry is situated.
            Aside from having a lagging infrastructure, India continues to be stigmatized by its
      stifling bureaucracy, red tape, corruption, and set of rigid labor rules that makes it quite
      difficult for companies to lay off employees. Unless these deficiencies and administrative
      problems are corrected, India will have great difficulty achieving world-class economic
      status.
            If the government fails to follow up with the needed public investments, it will stunt
      the economy’s growth for years and probably bring higher rates of inflation. On the other
      hand, if officials allocate enough resources to improve roads, ports, electrical generation,
      and airports, as well as reduce bureaucratic delays, the benefits will be lasting and signifi-
      cant. Whichever course the country takes, the results will show up in the macroeconomic
      data, particularly with industrial production and inflation. To monitor these and other key
      economic indicators of India, one can go online to the Ministry of Statistics—specifically,
      the Central Statistical Organization (CSO).
            The latest data on the major macroeconomic indicators has been assembled on one
      page, found at http://mospi.nic.in/Mospi_New/site/inner.aspx?status=3&menu_id=84.
            The Web page breaks down as follows:
       1. GDP at current prices.
       2. GDP at constant prices. (To view the entire press release of the latest quarterly GDP
          report, go to http://mospi.nic.in/Mospi_New/upload/mospi_press_releases.htm?
          status=1&menu_id=120.)
       3. The key components of GDP.
       4. Industrial production: Total and broken down by its three major segments: mining,
          manufacturing, and electricity. But more revealing are the three main categories of
          product: capital goods, intermediate goods, and consumer goods.
       5. Inflation: The CSO publishes a dizzying array of inflation measures, seven to be exact.
          They are the GDP implicit price index, no fewer than five variants of consumer price
          inflation, and the wholesale price index (WPI).
          The implicit price index is a quarterly measure and thus is not especially timely. Of the
          five CPI measures, the three most useful are the recently introduced groupings of CPI
          Urban (which is based on surveys taken from 310 towns), CPI rural (based on 1,181
          villages across India), and the combined CPI (a series that began in 2012 and serves as
          the headline retail price inflation in the country). The newly constructed national CPI
          will likely replace the wholesale price index as the main benchmark for monetary pol-
          icy action by India’s central bank. For years, the Reserve Bank of India had relied on
          the wholesale price index as a barometer of price pressures in the country. But critics
          complained that the WPI often understated inflation because it looked only at product
                         India: Industrial Production and Inflation                       407



   prices at the wholesale level and largely ignored the cost of services, a sector that plays
   an increasingly important role in the economy. Economists in India took note of how
   the rest of the world focused on the CPI because it ultimately reflected prices to the end
   user, namely consumers. As a result, we believe that the three CPI measures will in
   time overshadow the WPI as the best leading indicator of monetary policy.
6. Wholesale Price Index (WPI): India’s WPI is similar to the Producer Price Index in
   other countries. It is sensitive to price changes in commodities and industrial goods but,
   as stated previously, has little representation in services.

 BRAZIL’S INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION AND THE IBC-BR
             ECONOMIC ACTIVITY INDEX
      What Is It: Two important economic statistics on Brazil. The first reflects
          industrial output, and the second is considered a leading indicator of the
          country’s GDP.
      News Release on the Internet:
          Industrial Production: www.ibge.gov.br/english/presidencia/default_ant.php
          and www.bcb.gov.br/?INDICATORS
          IBC-Br Economic Activity Index: www.bcb.gov.br/?INDICATORS
      Release Time:
           Industrial Production: 9:30 a.m.(local time); the report is released about 40
           days after the survey month ends. (Thus, January’s release refers to industrial
           performance in November.)
           IBC-Br Economic Activity Index: 10:20 a.m. (local time); published about 45
           days after the reference month.
      Frequency: Monthly.
      Sources: Brazilian National Statistics Institute, Brazilian Institute for Geography
           and Statistics (IBGE), and the Central Bank of Brazil.
      Revisions: Both reports are subject to revisions.
      There is no country on the planet—not a single developing or industrial nation—that pos-
      sesses the near-perfect set of attributes Brazil has. And if you suspect I’m guilty of hyper-
      bole here, think again. Brazil may be classified as an emerging economy, but it also has as
      a well-diversified industrial sector—including one of the largest aerospace industries in
      the world, a major auto producer, a global-size energy company—and has the engineering
      know-how and resources to even build a nuclear submarine. But let’s not stop there.
      Brazil is endowed with a mind-boggling array of physical and natural resources, thanks to
      the Amazon basin. It is energy self-sufficient (a fact that bears repeating for emphasis),
      has ample arable land, possesses massive offshore oil fields, enjoys a benign climate, is
      gifted with thousands of miles of magnificent beaches, and is surrounded by other demo-
      cratically elected developing nations. To many foreign investors, Brazil just about defines
      what the “promised land” should look like.
           The country thus has all the prerequisites to become a prosperous leader in the global
      economy, and that has not escaped the attention of foreign investors. Indeed, many look
      upon Brazil as having even greater economic potential than the two Asian giants. China
      might have matchless human assets with 1.3 billion people (versus Brazil’s more modest
      200 million citizens), but it also is rapidly running out of critical natural resources. India
      has a large population and a fast-growing economy, but it too is highly dependent on
      imports of oil and other vital commodities. Looked at in terms of per capita GDP (a way
                 Brazil’s Industrial Production and the IBC-Br Economic Activity Index         411



    of measuring a country’s standard of living), Brazil recorded a per capita GDP of $11,769
    in 2011, far higher than that of China ($8,382) and three times that of India ($3,694),
    according to the IMF.
          In many respects, Brazil is already a star player in the global arena. It has just sur-
    passed Britain to become the world’s sixth-largest economy. Closer to home, Brazil easily
    outweighs its neighbors in economic size, accounting for more than 40% of Latin
    America’s total GDP.
          Facilitating all this progress have been the political and economic reforms the coun-
    try has undertaken the past three decades. After more than half a century of strong mili-
    tary influence in the government, the country made a fateful transition to mass electoral
    democracy in the mid-1980s. This shift was all the more remarkable because it occurred
    smack in the middle of the Latin American debt crisis. In addition to establishing a vigor-
    ous democracy with a multiparty system, Brazil’s leaders have liberalized the domestic
    capital markets. They allowed their currency to float in foreign exchange markets, crafted
    a new fiscal spending plan, opened the economy to more competition, embarked on a pri-
    vatization program, and passed legislation to further deregulate the economy. Moreover,
    in a bold forward-looking move, policymakers successfully placed the country on a path
    toward energy independence. Brazil’s ethanol program, along with newfound oil, trans-
    formed the country from being a net importer of oil in the 1980s to one that is energy
    self-sufficient in 2006, and now destined to be a major oil exporter.
          The results for Brazil’s economy have been palpable. The country has weathered
    global economic downturns better than its neighbors. While the U.S. and Europe strug-
    gled with recession after the tech-bubble burst of 2000 and 2001, economic activity in
    Brazil continued to expand without interruption. It even weathered the global financial
    downturn of 2008–09 with relatively minor damage. The country was one of the last to
    fall into recession in 2008 but among the first to resume growth in 2009. In fact, Brazil’s
    GDP bounced back with a robust 7.5% growth rate in 2010 and a respectable 2.7% in
    2011 (beating out the performance of the U.S. and Europe).
          Still, Brazil needs to do more. Its central bank, which carries out monetary policy,
    does not yet have full independence and thus can be subject to political influence. The
    country continues to have severe social problems due to sharp inequalities in its income
    distribution. It also has a creaky infrastructure that requires attention, and it needs to fur-
    ther reform its judicial system.
          But make no mistake: Brazil’s economy is on the move and international investors
    have eagerly returned to help expand the country’s industrial and service sectors. Anyone
    monitoring economic activity in Brazil has to focus on at least two key indicators: indus-
    trial production and the IBC-Br Economic Activity Index.

INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION
    The first important indicator is industrial production, which represents 27% of the coun-
    try’s GDP (with services contributing 67% and agriculture 6%). To measure industrial
412            Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?



      output, the government surveys 8,500 establishments on the output of 900 different prod-
      ucts. Brazil’s Institute for Geography and Statistics (IBGE) compiles the data, announces
      the news, and publishes an online press release in English. There are two excellent online
      sources to view the latest data on Brazil’s industrial production.
           One source is IBGE’s Web site (www.ibge.gov.br/english/presidencia/
      default_ant.php), shown here.




            Another government agency, the Central Bank of Brazil (www.bcb.gov.br/
      ?INDICATORS), does a slightly better job of presenting the industrial production tables
      along with other important economic indicators—though without any accompanying
      commentary. What’s more, the information has to be downloaded onto a spreadsheet, but
      it’s a step well worth the effort.
                 Brazil’s Industrial Production and the IBC-Br Economic Activity Index     413



        After the data is downloaded from Brazil’s central bank, the top part of the page
    notes the monthly value-added index of industrial production, and the bottom has all the
    percentage changes with the following time frames:
        • The latest monthly change (using seasonally adjusted figures).
        • Change over the past 12 months (using the observed data, not seasonally adjusted).
        • Change in the year so far versus the same period the previous year (using observed
          data).
        • Change in the past 12 months from the prior 12 months (using observed data).
        The page also breaks down industrial production as follows:
        • General industrial production index: An overall snapshot of industrial output.
        • Capital goods: An indicator that tells whether companies are investing.
        • Intermediate goods: A helpful leading sign of future production.
        • Consumer durable goods: A category that consists of household appliances and
          home electronics.
        • Consumer nondurable goods: Here we refer mainly to food and clothing. Both con-
          sumer durable and nondurable goods output are linked to the growth in wages and
          personal income.


THE IBC-BR ECONOMIC ACTIVITY INDEX
    The second key indicator on Brazil is the IBC-Br Economic Activity Index
    (www.bcb.gov.br/?INDICATORS). It’s published monthly by Brazil’s central bank and is
    closely watched by analysts who consider it a reliable leading indicator of the country’s
    quarterly GDP performance. The Economic Activity Index was originally released as a
    regional statistic, but the central bank expanded its coverage to the national economy in
    2010. The index now incorporates estimates for the monthly output of Brazil’s three sec-
    tors—industrial, services, and agriculture—and computes an index using a methodology
    similar to calculating the GDP. By tracking both industrial production and the Economic
    Activity Index, investors can get an excellent overview on the health of the Brazilian
    economy and its likely direction.

                           CANADA:
              INTERNATIONAL MERCHANDISE TRADE

               IVEY PURCHASING MANAGERS INDEX
      What Is It: Three economic measures on Canada that move markets.
      Home Web Address for Statistics Canada: www.statcan.gc.ca/
           start-debut-eng.html
      Home Web Address for Ivey Purchasing Managers Index:
           http://iveypmi.uwo.ca/english/index.htm

           International Merchandise Trade: 8:30 a.m. (ET); released the second week

      We have all heard of the “stress tests” that regulators imposed on U.S. banks recently to
      determine whether they can survive future economic shocks. The tests involve putting
      banks through a series of near-cataclysmic scenarios to see how financially sturdy they
      are. It’s an imperative exercise to prevent future bailouts by taxpayers. But here’s a ques-
      tion: Why waste a perfectly horrendous financial crisis? Let’s look back and see which
      major industrial economies and banks came out of the 2008–09 global catastrophe rela-
      tively unscathed. After all, that event was the ultimate stress test, so wouldn’t it be
      interesting to see who passed through this devastating experience with minimal damage?
           It turns out only two advanced countries came through in good form, Canada and
      Australia. We’ll begin with Canada and discuss Australia in the next section.
           What is so appealing about Canada is its enormous economic diversity and overall
      financial soundness—a combination all too rare these days. By economic diversity, I
      mean to highlight both the wealth of its natural resources and the country’s highly skilled
      workforce in manufacturing and services. When it comes to financial soundness, we look
      to the integrity of the banking industry, because no economy can function well without a
      vibrant group of banks to help finance economic activity. Let’s view each separately.
           Canada’s economy can be divided into three distinct sectors: resources, manufactur-
      ing, and services.
               Canada: International Merchandise Trade, Composite Leading Indicators,        417
                                  Ivey Purchasing Managers Index

RESOURCES
    That it has such a vast assortment of natural resources should not come as a complete sur-
    prise since the country has the second-largest landmass in the world (exceeded only by
    Russia). Central and western Canada in particular have seen rapid growth in the produc-
    tion of oil, lumber, diamonds, gold, nickel and uranium—to make the short list. Yet even
    parts of eastern Canada, like Newfoundland and Labrador, areas that long relied on the
    fishing industry for income, are now leading the way with new oil and gas exploration.
    And it is all paying off. Canada has the third-largest proven oil reserves in the world
    (more than Kuwait and Russia combined). It is also the eighth-largest oil exporter, ship-
    ping more crude than half the OPEC countries.

MANUFACTURING
    Aside from its abundance of resources, Canada also has a huge manufacturing base, the
    biggest of which is the production of autos, thanks to its ties with the U.S. motor vehicle
    industry. Although Canada’s auto sector has gotten much of the spotlight, foreign
    investors are keenly aware of the country’s other major producers, such as agricultural
    machinery, oil and gas drilling equipment, pharmaceuticals, high-tech electronics, and
    shipbuilding.

SERVICES
    Where Canada has recently impressed observers the most is in the strength and stability
    of its financial services sector. When the world economy tanked in 2008–09, many large
    international banks would have collapsed had governments not come to their rescue with
    prodigious injections of capital. Bank bailouts were particularly extensive in the U.S.,
    Britain, Germany, and Netherlands, and in one case, Iceland, the banks had to be nation-
    alized. But there was no such government assistance for the Canadian banks. No taxpayer
    bailout was needed here. No special entity had to be created to buy toxic assets.
         What made Canada’s banking system stand out? First, it has always been more
    tightly regulated than banks in the U.S. or Europe. For instance, Canadian banks are not
    permitted to make high-risk loans, such as adjustable-rate mortgages with five-year teaser
    rates, a practice that was common in the U.S. and ended up shocking American borrowers
    once rates rebounded. In contrast, when Canadian banks issued variable-rate mortgages,
    they would adjust the rates daily to conform to the market. Second, Canadian banks were
    better capitalized than their American and European counterparts. Third, lenders in
    Canada displayed a different management style. They were much more risk-aversive,
    avoiding subprime mortgages and other less-creditworthy borrowers. Perhaps the single
    biggest factor that kept the Canadian banks out of trouble was their practice of holding on
    to the mortgages they originated, a policy that prompted them to make prudent lending
    decisions from the start. If those mortgages failed, the banks themselves would suffer the
    consequences. But U.S. banks scoffed at such a practice. Why be cautious at all? U.S.
418            Chapter 4 • International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?



      lenders chose not to hold on to the mortgages they originated. Instead, those loans were
      quickly packaged with other mortgages, converted into highly complex securities, and
      sold to unsuspecting investors. These concocted instruments ended up causing an enor-
      mous real estate and mortgage bubble that eventually triggered a historic economic and
      financial meltdown. Although Canada also slipped into recession briefly in 2009, the
      downturn proved much less severe than in most other countries. But what wowed many
      investors and policymakers was the inherent strength of its financial sector. Canada’s
      banks came to be recognized as the strongest in the world.
           To be sure, Canada’s economy has some vulnerabilities. Its impressive industrial
      capabilities and immense natural resources have led to a rush of foreign investment into
      the country, and that has lifted the value of the Canadian dollar to levels that have chal-
      lenged exporters.
            In addition, Canada’s economy is still very closely tied to the U.S., thanks largely to
      the 1989 Canada Free Trade Agreement and the 1994 North American Free Trade
      Agreement. Indeed, a change in interest rates by the U.S. Federal Reserve can affect both
      countries, since 75% of Canada’s exports (mostly autos and parts, agriculture products,
      and oil) are destined for the U.S. Yet Canada has also taken concrete steps to expand its
      trading relationship with other countries. Merchandise trade with China, for example, has
      more than tripled in just the past ten years.
           For all the reasons cited above, there will continue to be growing interest in Canada’s
      financial and real economy by investors. To best track business activity in the country,
      one can turn to the government’s main economic Web site, Statistics Canada. While some
      access to its database requires payment, there are also several valuable sites within
      Statistics Canada that are freely available.
         • Main Free Site for Statistics Canada

                                 AUSTRALIA:
                              CONSUMER PRICES
                                RETAIL TRADE
                            INTERNATIONAL TRADE
      What Is It: Three critical baramoters on Australia’s economic health.
      Most Current News Release on the Internet:
           Consumer Prices: www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/6401.0/
           Retail Trade: www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/8501.0
          International Trade: www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/5368.0
      Home Web Address: www.abs.gov.au/
      Release Time:
           Consumer Prices: Quarterly, 11:30 a.m., local time; published the last full
           week in January, April, July, and October, and refers to the preceding quarter.
           Retail Trade: Monthly, 11:30 a.m., local time; usually published the first
           week of the month and covers retail sales two months earlier.
           International Trade: Monthly, 11:30 a.m., local time; released the first or
           second week of the month and covers trading activity two months earlier.
      Source: Australia Bureau of Statistics.
      Only one advanced economy successfully sidestepped the 2008–09 global financial
      wreckage: Australia. While the U.S. and Europe faced the worst economic collapse since
      the 1930s, business “down under” just kept humming along. In fact, the last time
      Australia slipped into recession was in 1991, which means the country has enjoyed unin-
      terrupted growth for more than 20 years. That’s one of the longest periods of continuous
      economic expansion ever recorded.
           How has the country managed to pull this off? We know that the business cycle has
      not been outlawed in the South Pacific. So was this extraordinary stretch of growth due to
      luck—or clever design? The answer is, a lot of both.
           In terms of luck, Australia inherited several bonuses. For example, although its cul-
      tural and geopolitical ties are firmly rooted in the West, its geographic proximity to the
      world’s fastest-growing economies enabled Australia to lock up some very lucrative trade
      deals. What countries, like China and India, need most to fuel their supercharged
      economies are vast quantities of raw material. And it just so happens that Australia is
      well endowed with precisely the kind of natural and industrial commodities its neighbors
      most need.
           Australia’s well-being, however, was also the result of design. The Reserve Bank of
      Australia (RBA), for instance, has pursued a cautious monetary policy. When most other
      central banks rushed to slash short-term rates to near zero during the 2008–09 global
                 Australia: Consumer Prices, Retail Trade, International Trade           423



downturn and then followed with more unconventional forms of monetary easing, the
RBA chose not to follow suit. Instead, it pursued a more modest approach, never allowing
the benchmark cash rate to fall below 3%. That careful, deliberate approach helped avoid
the kind of debt and housing bubble that plagued so many Western countries. Credit must
also be given to Australia’s financial institutions. Bank managers were always more con-
servative in their lending practices and never succumbed to the temptation of making a
fast buck by building up excessive leverage or recklessly dishing out mortgages, actions
that brought crippling losses to Wall Street. All that good governance by Australian banks
paid off. When most of the world was seized by a global credit crunch late in the last
decade, Aussie banks kept their strong credit ratings and thus were easily able to raise
capital to buttress their balance sheets.
     Australia’s leaders also acted smartly with a well-timed economic stimulus package
to keep the economy out of trouble. Arguably the most effective actions that set Australia
on the right course were the sweeping structural reforms introduced in the 1980s and
1990s. Those changes loosened up the domestic economy, carefully deregulated the
financial sector, lowered import tariffs, allowed the Australian dollar to float, and reduced
barriers to allow more foreign capital into the country. All these factors have helped insu-
late Australia against economic shocks, kept the country’s jobless rate low (it helps when
you have a population of just 23 million), and provided the backdrop for a vibrant finan-
cial services sector.
     If there is one popular explanation why foreign investors have found Australia so
compelling, it is how the country has hitched its economy to the growth prospects of
China, India, Indonesia, and South Korea, and yet still maintains large trading ties with
the U.S., Japan, and the U.K.

           But one also has to be careful here. Could Australia’s economy be too dependent on
      the growth of its Asian trading partners? What if economic activity slows markedly in
      this region? Another concern is the large amount of foreign capital inflows. True, it is a
      sign of confidence in Australia, but the flood of money entering the country can become
      problematic too. By having an open economy, capital inflows can push up the value of the
      Australian dollar, drive property prices higher, and heat up inflation pressures—all of
      which could slow GDP growth. This is why investors must remain vigilant in monitoring
      the country’s economic statistics. The best source for such data is the Australian Bureau
      of Statistics. Although they publish hundreds of economic indicators, here are some of
      the most sensitive for the financial markets:
          • To begin with, you can get a quick look at Australia’s very latest economic barom-
            eters here:
            www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/ViewContent?readform&view=
            ProductsbyReleaseDate&Action=Expand&Num=1.1
          • Snapshots of all its key macroeconomic indicators and their statistics are shown on
            this Web page:
            www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/1345.0

         • Consumer Price Index (Not Shown)
           Most industrial countries release CPI figures every month. Australia, however, pub-
           lishes inflation data on a quarterly basis. The government relies on about 10,500
           respondents to get 100,000 different price quotations, and then prepares a 36-page
           report on retail price inflation.
           www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/6401.0/

         • Retail Trade
           Are Australian consumers still in a spending mood? The answer has a major influ-
           ence on the stock and bond market. A sharp escalation in expenditures can drive
           inflation higher and force the central bank to act. In contrast, a dramatic and sus-
           tained slowdown in consumer outlays can also be worrisome since it could worsen
           unemployment, hurt corporate profits, and cut GDP growth. This measure compares
           total sales of goods and services in retail stores in Australia (but excludes auto
           sales).
           www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/mf/8501.0
           (1) The 24-page retail sales report divides the data into three parts: “Original,”

               Of the three, the seasonally adjusted and trend data warrant close watching.
